speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, May 18, 1951, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) asked me to explain the difference between certain amounts that were given in answer to questions put by two hon. members concerning the site for the printing bureau in Hull. The answer is a lengthy one, but I think I should put it on Hansard.
The Federal District Commission Act, 1927, chapter 55 of the statutes of 1927, was amended by chapter 51 of the statutes of 1946 to provide for the establishment of the national capital district, which is defined in the amending act as the national capital district established pursuant to this act.
The responsibility for selecting the location of sites, inter alia, for public buildings within the confines of the national capital district is vested in the federal district commission by virtue of section 6A of the said act as amended in 1946.
The national capital planning committee was established by the federal district commission, under authority of order in council P.C. 1266 of April 18, 1946, for the purpose of drawing up a master plan for the development, improvement and beautification of the national capital district.
By letter dated December 5, 1946, directed to the Minister of Public Works, the chairman of the federal district commission advised that upon the advice of the national capital planning committee the federal district commission had' recommended the expropriation of a property in the city of Hull by the dominion government, the commission having approved the site for the erection thereon of the printing bureau and other departmental buildings incidental to the future building development, the said site being described by the commission as follows:
That area bounded on the north by Brewery creek, on the east by Maisonneuve street, on the south by Boulevard Sacre Coeur to St. Henri street to Marsden property line to St. Redempteur street
to Elgin street to Brewery creek, saving and excepting the property already owned and occupied by the Reverend Oblate Fathers.
The expropriation of the above described area, as approved by the federal district commission, was further authorized by the governor in council under P.C. 842, dated March 6, 1947.
The first question referred to by the leader of the opposition in sessional paper 107-D, dated May 17, 1951, as asked by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness), was as follows:
How much was paid for the site on which the building is being erected?
The answer is as follows:
Estimated cost, $496,817.56.
The figure contained in this answer is an estimate covering the cost of the acquisition of land acquired for the purpose of the erection of the printing bureau proper, and is exclusive of the land contiguous thereto that was acquired for the purpose of future building development in accordance with the approval of the federal district commission. Of this estimated cost, the sum of $455,080 has to date been paid. The balance of $41,737.56 is the estimated cost of the settlement covering the remaining lands in the printing bureau site proper as aforesaid.
The second question referred to by the leader of the opposition in sessional paper 107-B dated March 27, 1950, as asked by the hon. member for Victoria, Ont. (Mr. Hodgson), was as follows:
What was the cost of the site of the proposed printing bureau in Hull, Quebec?
The answer was:
Cost of the site to date, $824,979.72.
The figure contained in this answer represents the cost at that date of the lands acquired in accordance with the recommendation and approval of the federal district commission for the purpose of erecting thereon a printing bureau and development of the contiguous area for government buildings in the future. The figure is, of course, not exhaustive of the cost of the acquisition of the entire area, but will be supplemented in accordance with the adjudication by the exchequer court, or settlement reached, as the case may be.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Last night I outlined the provisions that had been made in the estimates to provide assistance to the provinces as a result of our agreement in February last with the provinces in respect to the standardization of hose couplings. The hon. member asked me particularly as to the procedure to be followed. The procedure would be for the civil defence authority, in this case the minister of social welfare in Quebec, to advise as to the priority claim of a community in relation to the over-all plan. As a result of that information there would be negotiations between the federal and provincial governments to provide assistance along the lines I have indicated.

Last night the minister agreed to furnish to the committee a functional break-down of the present staff, and I presume that he will also be in position to furnish a break-down of the functions of the staff as previously proposed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
First of all there is the civil defence co-ordinator, who is assisted by an administrative officer, grade 1; an administrative officer, grade 3; two administrative officers, grade 6; an administrative officer, grade 7; three technical officers; eight technicians; one messenger; three clerks; five stenographers; six typists.
There are 32 positions available, but as I said last night, there are only 27 filled. In addition there are a cook, storeman, cleaners and helpers at the school here in Ottawa. As I said last night, plans exist for 60 others but there has not yet been final determination as to these; it would depend on circumstances.

Surely some thought must have been given to the functional distribution of the enlarged personnel that was apparently involved in the first plans of the government in connection with this matter. When this question was first raised last night the Minister of National Defence said that the staff was to be 80. Now the Minister of National Health and Welfare has indicated that 27 positions have been filled, and he cannot say what will be done about the others. When thought was; first given to this matter and something was done that led to

Supply-National Defence a tentative decision to have a staff of 80, surely some planning was done or thought given to the functional distribution of the 80. Cannot the minister give us any information in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I gave it last night. As I have said, there are 32 positions available on the staff of the civil defence group as such. When civil defence was under my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, he did not have the personnel in his department that we have in the Department of National Health and Welfare. He had to give consideration to filling positions with persons such as we have in large measure in the Department of National Health and Welfare. I have not indicated the extent to which the 60 remaining posts will be filled in accordance with the plans which were conceived before the transfer took place. That will be decided upon in the light of circumstances as we see them. I can give no more complete answer than that.

I think it is most regrettable that the minister cannot give us more information. Surely he can tell us what work will be assigned to individuals if these other positions are to be filled, or how many personnel from his own department are going to fulfil the functions in whole or in part of civil defence administration. Surely there is information of that kind available.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I have already given it in
principle, but I shall give it again. The original intention was that preliminary training of civil defence officials would be done in Ottawa. There have been three courses at the school since January. Since that time some thought has been given to the problem, and it would seem-this is not the final decision-best to decentralize the training apart from the technical instructions which we will continue to give. The school in the province of Quebec started today, and two other provinces are opening schools. The result is that it will not be necessary for us to have as many instructors as we had originally contemplated, nor will it likely be necessary to have as many employees at the school, in the way of cooks and the like, to work along with the inevitable stenographic staff, and so on. If we carry out the present policy of decentralization we shall not need as many personnel in that particular. It is circumstances of this kind that have to be looked at.

Mr. Chairman, I should like
to proceed with the question I was asking yesterday. In the first place, I want to say to the minister that he rendered a great

service to the Canadian people when he awakened them in the stirring speech he made not so long ago. Now that the Canadian people have been awakened to the danger of war, they wrant to know what to do with regard to civil defence.
Last night the minister indicated that the procedure for any community to follow would be to get in touch with the provincial representative who had been appointed to look after civil defence within the province. My interpretation of his remarks has been approved by the minister. During the last war the civil protection in the House of Commons consisted of placing sandbags on each of the floors near the elevators. Later, in order to improve the situation, wooden boxes were provided, painted red, in which the sandbags were placed. That was supposed to provide fire protection for this fireproof building in time of war. I remember I brought one of those sandbags to Mitch Hepburn and he could not believe that that was the kind of protection we had in the House of Commons. Finally before the end of the war the boxes and the sandbags in them were taken away.
Civil defence is a much more serious thing than some people believe it to be. I take it seriously myself, and I give credit to the minister for his effort. I agree that he has one of the most difficult jobs of anyone in the government at the present time. We have heard for years about the danger of war at this spot in Europe, that spot in Asia or the other spot in Africa. All over the world there are danger spots. The newspapers for a long time have been printing stories to the effect that we may have war at any moment. We must be ready for it. I am extremely glad that the minister is in charge of civil defence in this country.
The minister spoke about hose couplings. I do not see the use of hose couplings without hose. This morning I telephoned to the bureau of statistics to ask them if they had any information about the length of fire hose available in each municipality. The answer was:	We have no information. I was not
at all surprised at that answer. Now that the minister has spoken about hose couplings, I will ask him if he has any information about the length of fire hose available in each municipality of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I am afraid that, offhand, I
could not answer that question; but I should be glad to try to get for my hon. friend as quickly as possible the information he has requested.

I thank the minister, and I agree with him. But may I tell him that if

the chief co-ordinator were worth his salt, the first thing he would have done with his stenographers, his skeleton staff and the others, would have been to write mimeographed letters to the various city clerks or city treasurers asking them what they already had in the way of protection against fire; because in the event of war, the greatest hazard is destruction by fire.
You will get that information in the next census.

At any rate, my hon. friend agrees with that. So long as he agrees with it, I am satisfied.
What is important for the chief co-ordinator and his staff to do is to come down to earth and to use a little bit of common sense and a little bit of perspicacity in their dealing with this problem, which is a difficult one because of the size of the country. It is impossible to copy what is being done in England for civilian protection, in view of the fact that the area of Canada is ten or twenty times greater than that of England. Our problems are entirely different. The United States have a much larger population than we have, and our problem is different from that in the United States. What the co-ordinator should do, under the able direction of the minister, would be to use his own judgment in considering local conditions in Canada as they should be considered in order to face the problem as it must be faced.
Suppose that I am in charge of civilian protection in my community. Any member may be in that position, or anyone else may be. Suppose I get in touch with the provincial representative who has authority within the province. There is not enough fire hose available. I write to him. He gets in touch with Ottawa and he does not get the hose; he gets couplings. What can we do with couplings without hose? If the department has bought such a large quantity of couplings, I wonder from whom it has bought them. Who is the manufacturer or the inventor of that device? How is it that the department is buying so many couplings and no hose at all?
Then there are to be considered the necessary water connections by means of which to fill the fire hose with water in order to fight a fire. What are those facilities in each municipality? I wonder if the minister has some information about that matter, through the ohief co-ordinator.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend will agree, since he asks me the question directly, that it is important to recognize, as he himself has said, that our situation in Canada is not the same as that in the United Kingdom.
Supply-National Defence The United Kingdom is a unitary state. Here we operate not only through the municipalities but also under the federal character of our country through the provinces. Fire protection is primarily a matter for the provinces and for the municipalities. The question that my hon. friend has asked, quite properly, in his zeal and his interest in this matter, is one which I am sure he will agree should also be addressed to another authority.
We have had to recognize the federal character of our country in trying to build up an organization, as he himself in his remarks so far has suggested we should. We have had a meeting with the provinces. We have pointed out to them, as they have pointed out to us, that one of the great hazards-particularly in respect of potential atomic attack, let us say, or bombing-would be the resultant fires and that more damage and destruction can come from fires than from anything else. We have said: How can we assist in providing for the greatest amount of mutual aid? That is what will be required if a disaster should come; and we all pray that it will not.
The situation is that the hose coupling is an extremely important factor, because there is no standardization throughout the country. The aim of the provinces-as a result of the decision which they themselves have come to through their fire marshals, their municipal bodies and so on

is that the federal government should give them some assistance in the installation of hose couplings in order to make it possible for community A to use the hose of community B, something which is not now possible in many cases because of a lack of standardization of the hose couplings. As to any community that may be short of hose itself, that is a matter on which no province has yet advised us that it requires financial assistance. I will note what my hon. friend has to say in that regard, and see what the situation is. But I am sure that with this brief explanation with regard to the standardization of hose couplings he will appreciate how important this matter is. It is not only important in one province; it is important as between one community and another on the border; in my own community, in Windsor, for instance, and in Detroit, and in the two Sault Ste. Maries. In those cases, by the use of adapters, it is possible to meet the problem that arises out of the lack of standardization.
I thank my hon. friend for what he has said about the other phase of the question, and I hope I have given him a satisfactory answer.

Supply-National Defence

I thank the minister for the good will he shows. When I ask questions about this matter it is because it is of vital importance. My constituents are interested in it, as are the constituents of every other member. It is not so much a question of money as of co-ordination with respect to the part Ottawa is to play under the authority of the minister himself. With regard to hose couplings, if the diameter of the hose is not standard how would it be possible to use couplings except of different sizes? And by the way, who manufactures those couplings; who is the inventor?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: There are many kinds of couplings. That is one of the problems in trying to get standardization.
I thank the minister again. Will these couplings be distributed by Ottawa to the provinces or to the municipalities?

No, Mr. Chairman. We are not providing the full cost of standardization of hose couplings. We have undertaken to provide one-third of the cost, with the provinces and municipalities to supply the balance, either the provinces alone or the two together. They will make their own purchases; they will decide as to the need. Those are questions we must leave to them, and which we propose to leave to them. This will be an assistance grant which will not completely cover the cost, the expenditure this year being in the neighbourhood of $900,000.

I thank the minister again, and I appreciate what he has said. In my humble view all possible information with respect to civil defence should be publicized to the limit. It cannot do harm to anyone, and it will help us all to know how the authorities, whether municipal, provincial or federal, will look after the protection of the Canadian people. If we spend $900,000 on hose couplings to be distributed by Ottawa to the provinces or the municipalities, or if we have a certain number of steel helmets, it will be impossible to distribute them in an emergency because that emergency may arise so quickly. Everything happens in such a little time, especially when jet planes are used. If a jet plane should attack any part of Canada, would it be possible to send hose couplings and helmets from Ottawa to the part of the country that was bombed? I do not think it would. I tell the minister again that it is not so much a question of money as one of good, plain common sense and co-ordination.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I am very glad the minister says hear, hear; and I mean co-ordination between all those interested in the protection of the country, which means everybody.
Now I am coming to another matter, in which I hope I shall have the support of the minister in charge of civil defence, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Defence Production and the Minister of Transport, because this matter concerns several departments. It is a fact that in any future war the best protection will be mobile units, and there are no units more mobile than the R.C.A.F. Therefore it is of vital importance to have airports at as many places as possible in this country. Many were built during the last war. We need many more good, large airports. In my humble view they would serve as a better protection for the country than any helmets or hose couplings or other devices of that kind.
In my county, for instance, we are 120 miles from Quebec city, where there is an airport; we are 80 miles from Mont Joli, where there is an airport; we are 100 miles from Caribou, Maine, where there is an airport. If I want to come to Ottawa by air I have to drive to Quebec city, a distance of 120 miles, or to Mont Joli, a distance of 80 miles, or to Caribou, a distance of 100 miles. There is no protection. For the protection of this country I hope the minister will discuss the matter with the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Defence Production and the members of the cabinet. For a time there was some discussion about the establishment of an airport at Cacouna in my constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It is a fine constituency, too- a lovely country.

I know, and it deserves protection, as does the whole country from Newfoundland to British Columbia, and especially Fraser valley, the garden of Eden of the west. The Minister of Defence Production told me one day in the railways and shipping committee that he wanted just a word from me with regard to the building of that airport, for which surveys had been made by the Department of Transport. That was in time of peace, and naturally there was an agitation about it. Now that we are in a period of emergency I hope the government will consider the matter anew and will not hesitate to build an airport at Cacouna according to the surveys and plans already made by the Department of Transport. No one will dare create any agitation about it, because it will be for the defence of this

country. If an airport is built in every constituency of Canada it will be the best way to protect Canadian people.
I am not going to insist further because the ministers who are here now realize the importance of the matter. The Prime Minister, who lives in my constituency during the summer, knows how important it is. I hope that will be done at the earliest possible opportunity, and I will defend the action of the government just as I would defend a similar action in any constituency in Canada. I will ask the minister of civil defence as well as the Minister of National Defence to tell the committee what they think about my suggestion.

As I listened to the hon. member for Temiscouata I wondered what the coupling would finally be coupled to; I knew there would be something for Temiscouata before he concluded.
The minister mentioned the fact that our country is different from a unitary state in that we have the federal system; that is perfectly true. But the United States also has the federal system. I intend to ask some questions relating to plans in the United States and to the extent to which the experience of the United States is being applied in Canada. The hon. member for Temiscouata said it is mainly a question of co-operation-
Co-ordination.

-co-ordination, and not the expenditure of money. I do not quite follow him in that. There are certain responsibilities of the federal authority. There may be a good reason why this very important subject of civilian defence was transferred from the Department of National Defence to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, but the reasons, other than the capacity of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, are not immediately apparent.
As I see the situation, this is one subject which particularly comes under the Department of National Defence. It is part and parcel of our plans and of the expenditure of this country for national defence. True enough, the final responsibility for providing personnel is a matter for the provinces and the municipalities. But in the national field the decisions as to shelters, medical stockpiles, the dispersion of industry, emergency housing and public works to facilitate civilian defence preparedness on a scale adequate to meet the expected needs, must fall upon the federal authority. I have discussed this matter with a number of mayors and councillors of municipalities, and I do not misinterpret their view when I suggest to the minister 80709-217
Supply-National Defence that, while they are prepared to supply voluntary personnel to meet the responsibility of fire fighting and the like within their respective municipalities, they are not receiving today the direction from the national authority that they have a right to expect.
The minister has only recently taken over the responsibility in this direction. He made a most persuasive and inspiring speech on the subject of civil defence. But more than that is required. The publication of the pamphlet to which he has made reference will go part of the way, but I feel that an intensive educational campaign must be launched by the federal authority. People do not want to believe there is going to be atomic bombing of Canada. The thought disturbs our equanimity. We like to look at the situation as though we were protected and insulated by many thousands of miles of sea and a northern ice cap. It is going to require an educational campaign to make the people realize the danger in which we find ourselves.
I looked up some of my clippings of a few years ago, and I have one here which I picked at random. It is dated April, 1948, and says "Big radar fence against aircraft". It went on to say that it was going to cost a great deal of money, several billions of dollars, and that it had been started in 1948. This is 1951, and the least said about that big radar fence the better. Those were some of the plans. Today the people have been lulled into a false sense of security. One of the lessons that came to me as one of the representatives of this parliament at the parliamentary conferences in Wellington and Canberra was a sense of deep foreboding as to the possibilities that faced our country, the other countries of the commonwealth, and the United States. Our people need to be aroused in this connection. Voluntary work has its place, but you can only get voluntary workers when, in the national field, there is the type of message given by the minister and other members of the government that will arouse the people to a realization that there are going to be no second chances this time.
The first point I bring to the attention of the minister is the need for direction and an educational campaign. Second, as to the matters to which I have referred, such as shelters, medical stockpiles, the dispersing of industry and the like, the responsibility rests upon the federal authority. It is all very well to say we have a distribution of authority among the federal, provincial and municipal governments. That is true, but the provision for civil defence in the national field must, as I say, rest upon the national authority. The only way in which that can be done is by grants in aid. I would not go before any

Supply-National Defence members of this government and ask for expenditures unless I believed the plans were either self-liquidating or necessary. An expenditure of $4-5 million this year is totally inadequate to meet the responsibilities with which we are faced. You cannot place that responsibility upon the municipalities. Today the municipalities are bearing rates of taxation that do not permit any further increase. National civil defence, administered on the provincial and municipal levels, means assistance in coping with the danger in which we find ourselves today as a nation.
One of the best articles I have read on this subject-I am not going to quote from it in extenso-is "The Defence of the Free World." It is a record of the proceedings of the academy of political science at a meeting held in November last. There is an article on the subject of civilian defence by the director of the New York state civil defence commission. He points out that we must realize one fact that was not generally admitted at this parliamentary conference. Most of the members were of the opinion that Russia had the atomic bomb. One of the representatives at that conference, who held a high position in the British -cabinet during the days of war, claimed that Russia did not have the atomic bomb. But the general consensus was that it had, and that it would be used without warning. That is the view taken by this authority who spoke at the meeting to which I have referred. He accepts the principle outlined by the minister, that the administration cannot be one of a central agency by itself. There must be the central agency for direction, but the basic responsibility for the carrying out of the national policy must rest with the -municipalities, under the direction of and in -co-operation with the provinces.
In the United States, detailed mutual assistance agreements have been entered into between states and between cities. The states of New York and New Jersey have entered into a joint agreement for -their defence, much as the northeastern cities bordering on the Pacific have entered into a joint pact binding on each of them. The general plans of the various states are coordinated in a national plan. But in this country, if we are to have something that is in keeping with the dangers that face us, the municipalities must receive a greater measure of assistance than is contemplated by the estimates now before this committee. The municipalities-and again I refer to the speech that was made before the political science association-have the responsibility of organizing volunteer welfare services to receive, feed, clothe, shelter and provide 
essential social services for evacuees in an orderly and efficient manner.
These local responsibilities can be discharged by the municipal authorities; for they have the agencies for them. They have the health department, the police force and the engineering organization in the respective cities. But in the larger field, in the field wherein national responsibility is preeminently of importance, I feel there has been too little assistance given nationally.
Before this session terminates I hope that the minister will be in a position to bring before the house a co-ordinated plan, which will provide for a larger measure of financing on the part of the national authority, and that financial assistance will be given through grants in aid provincially to the end that municipalities will not have added in their respective jurisdictions a financial burden which they cannot properly assume.
The other day I was speaking to a farmer in my own province of Saskatchewan. He pointed out the dangers inherent in communist infiltration in this country, and he brought to my attention something that I had never thought of before. He mentioned the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba-and the same applies agriculturally throughout the dominion-and the extent to which mechanization has taken place in the last fifteen years. Suppose war broke out tomorrow and the gasoline stocks in Saskatoon, Regina, Calgary and Edmonton were attacked. Where would there be production on the prairies with the mechanization we have today? That is one of the responsibilities involved in civil defence. It is a responsibility that is capable of being discharged by the municipalities through their police forces and through the setting up of voluntary police organizations. But before they do that they must receive from the federal government a national plan which may be co-ordinated and which will result, in place of the present haphazard plans, as they naturally are at this time, in a plan directed federally but administered through the provinces and the municipalities so far as detail is concerned, but dependent for its implementation on the national leadership.
Our people need to be aroused to the state of affairs existing at the present time. There is no more important problem before the Canadian people today than that of preserving our civilians; for they themselves will indeed be in- any front line. Should war come between Russia and the United States of America we would find ourselves in a desperate position. While the plans of 1948

were made and announced in eloquent terms, in 1951 we are little further ahead.
I want to say one thing more, Mr. Chairman. In the statements I have made there is no criticism of General Worthington or of his capacity and ability, or of the committees operating with him or of the various municipal defence authorities that have been set up. All that they have today is a general picture. They need a sense of direction from the national authority, and they need much greater financial support than is being given today.
Civil defence is as large a part of our national defence as is the obtaining of manpower and the production of the necessary sinews and munitions of war. It is for that reason that I suggest the Minister of National Defence give to the Minister of National Health and Welfare greater assistance than these estimates indicate is to be given.

I have been keenly interested
in what has been said about civil defence. We have talked about fire-fighting equipment and standardizing hose couplings. We have heard discussions about warning systems, decontamination, radiation detection, medical equipment and all that sort of thing, and it has all been interesting, timely-
But academic.

It is academic; that is true. I
listened with great interest to what the hon. member for Lake Centre said, and I must declare here, Mr. Chairman, that with practically everything he did say I found myself in agreement. I do not intend to repeat what has already been said in the debate. However, there is one thing that I should like especially to emphasize. After saying that not enough money has been voted or set aside this year for civil defence, I am quite certain-

May I interrupt for a moment? Constant reference is made to that. It would be very helpful to me if I could have some suggestions. I should like my hon, friend to know how much is being spent in the United Kingdom and how much is being spent in the United States. He would be very surprised to realize the extent to which in Britain they are spending. This year they are appropriating $20 million. In the United States the Senate is appropriating $86 million, and the House of Representatives $84 million. I ask my hon. friend to compare these figures, and particularly to compare the situation in Britain with what it is here.	.

This is not essentially a problem involving dollars and cents. The reason I rise at this time-I am sure my hon. friend will not mind-
Not at all.

The reason I rise at this time is that, as the minister responsible for civil defence, I am quite properly expected to try to give some leadership in the matter, and that I a,m endeavouring to do; but it would be unfair to insist on leadership on the one hand, and to say something on a matter with which I did not deal, unless I was given some proper direction.
I want my hon. friend to know that we have discussed this matter with the provinces. We have discussed this matter with the corresponding officials in Britain and in the United States. The plans that we are following are based upon consultations that we have had with the provinces, the United States and the United Kingdom. If in the light of our obligations, which primarily I believe must be to the armed forces in time of total war; if after providing for all these things, I believe in my heart-as I see the whole picture, as my advisers see it and as the government sees it-that more should be appropriated, I will not hesitate to make the necessary recommendations; but I do not propose to make a recommendation for the expenditure of any more money than is necessary.
I believe that the real emphasis is where I sought to place it, where Sir John Hodsoll, the greatest authority on civil defence in the world, because of his own experience, places it, namely, on the mutual aid principle, on every man and woman in this country or in the free world who has to face, unfortunately, the challenges of modern total war.

I thank the minister, and I appreciate this statement. But I still find myself thinking that perhaps some country in the world-and it might as well be the Canadian government as any other-will take the lead, and will not wait to find out what the United States has done or what Great Britain has done.
What do we care about comparisons? Let us look at the situation as if we were facing the real problem tomorrow. Let these other countries fiddle along, if that is what they want to do. I do not believe in that procedure, at all. I do agree with the minister however that there is no sense in appropriating and spending more money than is absolutely necessary for civil defence. But let us be sure that we spend as much as we should spend at this time, so that our people will be prepared.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I agree.

That is all I am concerned about. There is one practical aspect of the matter with which I should like to deal briefly- because I believe most other factors have been discussed fully. This practical aspect concerns the leadership that can be exercised by the government and by members of the House of Commons generally.
I was interested the other day in a statement emanating from Dr. William T. Salter of Yale university, who said:
The best protection against atom bomb attacks would be for everyone to pack blood plasma and bandages into a suitcase and go to live in the country.
Well, that is all very well for those who have a bag, in the first place, and who in the second place can afford blood plasma and bandages, and a place to live in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That would be the worst thing to do, in any event.

I did not find myself in too much agreement with that part of the statement. He did make a further statement however which, to my mind, is of importance, when he said:
We should follow a program of decentralization and of converting all our households into small granaries and medical units.
With that I thoroughly agree-and there are good reasons why. If we are wise we will counsel every Canadian family to make small granaries and medical units of their household. That is a practical thing that the people could do for themselves, if they were given just a little leadership and were offered a few suggestions. Some people, acting upon advice received from wise leaders, during the course of the last year or two, and at great pains, have accumulated a year's supply of certain foodstuffs which, today, they are constantly using and replacing. As I said, this was done painfully and at great sacrifice. They are using and replacing this supply today with newer material. An examination of what they have laid in will show that the permanent core of this store is a bushel or two of wheat in some sort of airtight metal container. That constitutes the small granary.
And a flour mill.
And perhaps a small flour mill, like one I now have. It is a well known fact that, with wheat and water-just those two things-human beings can survive almost indefinitely.
And a flour mill.

Yes, or even a small coffee grinder. With a little wheat and water a human being can exist in fair health for an


indefinite length of time. It seems to me the domestic store should contain not only the wheat in an airtight metal container, but water in stone or glass containers which would always be kept filled with fresh and clean water.
We all know one of the greatest dangers to any city in a time of air attack or bombing would be the contamination of the water supply. Under these circumstances it seems to me that one of the most practical things the minister and his staff could do would be to make the people of Canada in their homes, from one end of the country to the other, conscious of the necessity of doing something for themselves. And one of the best things they could do would be to set up in their own homes small granaries and medical units.
There has been considerable talk about hose couplings. Does the minister mean hose couplings or hydrant couplings? Surely he does not mean hose couplings?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes, we mean hose couplings.

But you do not need hose couplings unless you have hose. In Canada we do not have uniform hydrants in our different cities. What we need is couplings to fit the hydrants. I suggest we do not need hose couplings unless we have hose, but I am pointing out that we require different couplings for different types of hydrants. In one town or city we will find hydrants with threads differing from those in other towns and cities. Then, throughout the country, we find Old hydrants with couplings of different sizes. What we need is hydrant couplings, not hose couplings at all.
I will have my hon. friend's observations brought to the attention of all the provincial governments, who have asked for hose couplings.
It would seem that in the last while the minister has been getting into some difficulty and has been subjected to a good deal of criticism.
I thrive on it.

In this instance criticism is good, because there is no subject of greater importance than that of civil defence. Nothing could cause greater havoc in this country, nothing could bring about greater disruption in every sense than a poorly-organized civil defence.
In my view however the measure of success or failure in this respect must be the progress being made, and progress that we can see. While I listened to the debate I was wondering what actual and visual preparation is being made in, let us say, the city of Calgary. In the event of attack where would the people

of that city go and what would they do to seek assistance? It is not enough to say that we are preparing this or that, and that sooner or later we will have it done. The people should be aware of it now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: If that is a direct question I would answer from a report from the government of Alberta.
I should like to hear it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The government of Alberta advises us that a number of cities such as Edmonton, Calgary, Lethbridge and Medicine Hat are in an advanced stage in training- and then there is other information which, obviously, is quite secret. However, I would be prepared to show it to the hon. member privately. We are advised by the government of Alberta that civil defence directors have been appointed in these cities, and that the planning there has reached an advanced stage.

I am glad some cities in the country are making progress. Again, Alberta is taking the lead-with the assistance of the minister, of course. They are advising him, and perhaps helping people in the more backward cities of Canada to use that knowledge.
I have listened carefully to the discussion, but I have not heard reference made to the progress in connection with communications and transportation. We can talk all we like about preparations for civil defence, but without proper co-ordination between air, rail and highway transportation systems, we would be at a loss. No greater confusion could come about in the case of air attack than that which would be caused by lack of proper co-ordination between our transportation systems.
This was brought out clearly not so long ago when the railroad employees were out on strike. We saw then what might have happened without highway transportation. We would have been in a very bad position. In order to add to the effectiveness of the statement I have made I should like to quote from an article which appeared in "Bus and Truck Transport" magazine and which refers to statements that had been made by General Worthington, the civil defence co-ordinator. I think this article is so applicable that I should take the time of the committee to read it. This article appears on page 35 of the May issue and is entitled, "Ottawa forms defence transportation committee." A paragraph entitled, "Tremendous Problem" reads as follows:
Civil defence faces a "tremendous problem of transportation," General Worthington told the committee at its first meeting. The success or failure of civil defence in Canada could hinge on communications and transportation, he said.
Supply-National Defence A major function of transport would be the supply of aid to a devastated area from nearby communities. As well, it might be necessary to organize evacuation and to move great numbers of people over great distances. The wide separation of Canadian cities presented a problem not encountered in Europe, nor, to so great an extent, in the United States.
Where an area was chosen as a reception centre it was estimated that the number of people who could be taken in from other cities was 50 per cent of the area's normal population. That alone would be an immense problem and, for such emergencies, there must be an over-all co-ordinated plan.
"In the case of railways we must know where their rolling stock is and how best we can use it," General Worthington said. "In addition we have to face the fact that we may lose some parts of the railway system through enemy action and, in those cases, road transport must be ready to step in.
Air transport will be needed to bring in the most vital commodities to an attacked area-most likely medical supplies and medical personnel. This would be done by the heavier aircraft; lighter aircraft would be employed in air reconnaissance for fire fighting and, perhaps, highway traffic control." Turning to the role of road transport, General Worthington said two main needs were to arrange adequate fuel supplies and traffic control. "Police control inside the cities will probably not be too bad," he told the defence committee. "There will be civil defence traffic routes, and only authorized vehicles will be allowed to use them. But we will have to anticipate traffic jams on the open roads, away from target areas, because we feel that as soon as an attack begins, many people will jump into their private cars and the highways may become blocked. One job of this committee is to figure out how highway traffic can be controlled and kept moving."
Apparently a government-sponsored civil defence transportation committee was set up early last month in this city. It has held its initial meeting but I understand that it will not meet again until the latter part of July.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: One of the working committees is actually meeting this afternoon.
So far as I know the minister has not mentioned this very important subject of transport communications.

I mean the minister has not dealt with it in this debate.

I am glad the minister referred to the preparations being made in Alberta. In discussing this matter with cabinet ministers there I know that they are cognizant of the necessity of doing something and they have been working on this. Concrete results have been achieved. Mr. Chairman, at this
time I do not wish to pick a fight with anyone who holds views with respect to civil defence which may be diametrically opposed to those which I hold, but I do feel that the discussions so far-

I was called to order the other day and berated for speaking too


loudly. I have modulated my voice this afternoon so that I shall not offend the sensitive auricles of various hon. members of the committee. In that regard I might say that it is not often that in a matter of this kind I disagree with my good friend the hon. member for Lake Centre. But it seems to me that in the matter of civil defence we are now speaking in terms of dollars and cents. Personally, I do not believe that is the proper tactic for us to adopt at this time. I think it will be more or less universally agreed by everyone here that there is resting on the individual member of the House of Commons a responsibility which is as great as, if not greater than, that which rests on the government.
Certainly our plan of civil defence at the present time is not complete, and it is not perfect. I do not think that anyone in his right senses would expect it to be. But I would imagine that, in the near future, with the vote which it is now stated is going to be given to civil defence preparations, certain things will be brought about with respect to information for every hon. member. Rightly or wrongly, it is my considered opinion that the preparation and the successful carrying on of civil defence, as far as we are concerned, can best be accomplished in the 262 federal ridings of the Dominion of Canada by the members who sit in the House of Commons, provided they will go back to their constituencies and tell them what is needed after we have more information than we have at the present time and when the plan has gone forward to a more complete state of fruition than it has reached now. We should individually and collectively make it our bounden duty to see to it that we stress the importance of what is needful with respect to an adequate civil defence.
I do not think that the most essential factor in civil defence is the granting of a lot of federal money; but I believe that one of the essential factors is that the people have some information about the potential destruction in the event of an aerial attack. Let us put it this way. We know perfectly well that the destruction from the Hiroshima bomb was colossal. We know now-it is no secret- that had the victims of the Hiroshima bomb had adequate medical attention within forty hours or forty-eight hours, the casualties resulting from radiation would have been cut by at least 40 per cent. We also know that when you have atomic explosions-this is also no secret, and I am not quoting from any book-if there is a warning that is understood by all the people, atomic casualties will be cut by another 40 per cent. In my opinion, therefore, it is logical to conclude that one

of the first things that should be done by the members of parliament and the government is the giving of consideration to a universal system of warning that will be the same in Newfoundland as it is on Vancouver island, in the province of British Columbia, and all the intervening terrain.
How can we best bring about a decrease of casualties? I think it is generally known that in all the industrial areas of all the provinces of the Dominion of Canada we have the nucleus of a volunteer service that cannot be matched in any other country in the world. I refer now to that great body of men and women who are fully trained and qualified in first aid. In my opinion they can and ought to be considered a volunteer nucleus from which can develop in each locality across the Dominion of Canada a tremendously important factor in the reduction of casualties. That force is completely and entirely voluntary. It will not cost the government of Canada a dollar to put that force into operation. I am convinced that every man and woman in that group would be delighted to tutor, maybe once or twice a week, various groups in his or her particular community who would be able to carry on any first aid work in a most adequate manner.
With respect to atomic explosions, we also know that in hospital areas and congested metropolitan areas the likelihood of casualties among physicians will, in all probability, go to fifty per cent. If that is true-and I believe it is-then every one of us must do something with regard to the education of his constituency in that matter. (Let us consider my own riding in the city of Vancouver. It has the largest hospital in the province of British Columbia; I refer to the Vancouver general hospital. We have there a tremendous area of hospitalization. Suppose an atomic bomb should hit close to or upon the Vancouver general hospital. The loss in professional services-those both of nurses and of physicians and surgeons- would immediately be at least fifty per cent.
A great deal can be said for decentralization of hospitalization; but the fact remains that we must deal with the situation as it now is. The. hospital is there, the facilities are there, and the personnel are there; and they are going to remain there unless something in the nature of a flood or a holocaust of some sort or other occurs without Uncle Joe pulling the string. We must face the facts with respect to this whole situation. Candidly, I believe that we are about to get a great deal more information from our civic defence authorities. At the present time there is no
Supply-National Defence one in any part of Canada or the United States who can say that we have the complete blueprint for security in the event of an atomic explosion. But as individual members of the House of Commons we at least have a duty to perform when we go back to our constituencies, namely to give to the people what, in our opinion, might be the potential of an atomic explosion anywhere in our district. That is something for each of us to do. Certainly the government can help by giving the necessary information; but whether it is an atomic explosion, a flood or any other holocaust a great deal of the aid given in the first instance will be voluntary, coming from your next door neighbour.
This afternoon there was some mention of couplings, and one hon. member said he did not mean hose couplings but hydrant couplings. I am not going to enter that argument-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: There is no argument on that subject. Do not confuse the people.

We know perfectly well what happened at Rimouski not so very long ago. We also know what has happened in various parts of Canada during the last few years when great fires have occurred. The hydrant facilities in adjoining municipalities have not been co-ordinated. Certainly to standardize the threads on all hydrants across Canada would cost the taxpayers of this country hundreds of millions of dollars, and I do not think that expenditure would be justified. I do believe some consideration should be given, however, if it has not been given.' already, to the use of adapters that could be utilized on hydrants of adjoining municipalities where the threads are different. In many instances I believe that would reduce the number of casualties and would be a much cheaper way of giving adequate protection in the event of a large fire.
Furthermore, while I may be old fashioned in my ideas with respect to the response of the Canadian people in the event of attack, I think there is something in the spirit of the early pioneers on the prairies that could be adopted right across Canada in both rural and urban areas. On my way down to the opening of this session I stopped off in Saskatchewan to visit my brother. He has a huge barn, though I do not know whether it is as large as that of the hon. member for Springfield. As has been stated this afternoon, the farms across Canada have been largely mechanized, and many large barns are not used to anything like full capacity. I am as sure as that I am now speaking to you that in the event of any holocaust in Saskatchewan

Supply-National Defence -and I use that just as an illustration, for I am sure the same thing would apply from coast to coast-the neighbourliness that has been born of hardship and experience would be a tremendous factor in providing aid and assistance to those in need. We also know that in a good bank barn you are perhaps as well protected as you could be anywhere. In my view the voluntary aspect of civil defence is far more important than the expenditure of a large sum of money for the purchase of equipment which may not be used this year or within the next five years.
So I leave this thought with you, Mr. Chairman, for what it may be worth. I do not believe the government should be too severely condemned because some people, perhaps without adequate information, feel that the appropriation for civil defence is not large enough. To me the voluntary part of the program is much more worthy of consideration than the pouring of millions of dollars into equipment that may or may not be used. We know perfectly well that Uncle Joe is not going to telegraph and tell us if and when an atomic attack is going to occur. So I conclude on a note very similar to that on which I opened. If we are to adequately meet the needs of civil defence it must be particularly by way of voluntary effort. I do say the government should give the lead, and I am thoroughly convinced that the minister will do so, and will give every member of this house the necessary information so that we may go back and impress upon our constituents the importance of civil defence and the part to be played by voluntary effort. If we do that I am quite sure the response of the Canadian people will be adequate to meet the need. I am also sure that if the minister finds it necessary to increase this appropriation you and I as taxpayers will have no objection at all. We should always remember, however, that in these matters the neighbourly feeling counts for much more than a terrific expenditure of money.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I do not want to repeat what I have said already in my initial statement, but in the light of the discussion that has taken place I believe there are some things that will have to be said in the public interest.
I do not desire to shut off any hon. member, but I thought I should say now that I do intend to try to more or less close the matter and bring it to a head. If any hon. members wish to speak before I do so, they have a perfect right; I am just giving an indication of my intention. I believe many of the things that have been said have perhaps arisen because hon. members have not had an opportunity to really see what has been going on not only in Ottawa but in every province and [Mr. MacDougallJ

almost every major municipality. If anyone wishes to anticipate me, I am prepared to wait, but I should like to more or less summarize what I have to say in order to bring the discussion to a conclusion more readily than perhaps would otherwise be the case.

It is not my intention to speak on this subject at length. Last September I covered the different types of warfare as far as Canada is concerned. I dealt with gas and chemical warfare, explosive bombs, atomic bombs, and those things which might represent a danger to our country. I must say I was pleased last evening when the minister came out with a complete account of his expenditures. If we had been given that statement by the Minister of National Defence in the early part of the debate we might have been a good deal further along in the consideration of the estimates. For that part, I congratulate the minister. I was disturbed, though, last night by one part of his speech to which I should like to refer. He said, as reported at page 3387 of Hansard of May 24:
I am certain that as long as I am in charge of this difficult assignment I am not going to go ahead and build up an organization which in the event of disuse would rust and do more harm than good.
Further on he said:
We may make a big miscalculation; there can be no doubt of that possibility, but certain risks have to be taken in this matter. Those risks have to be borne not only by the armed forces but by everyone in Canada, for that is the nature of total war. No minister of the crown or anyone else can alter that unfortunate fact.
I said I was disturbed when I heard him use those words. I have read the statement several times this afternoon, and there seems to be a tone in the minister's speech which is suggestive of something like gambling. We are going to take a chance. In so far as the defence of this country and of our people is concerned, I do not believe we should ever take a chance. So far as money is concerned, let us compare the amounts allotted for this purpose. We are going to spend something like $5 billion on the armed forces for our defence, while we are going to spend something like $5 million for the defence of the people of this country. It is rather difficult to understand this, because the conditions of warfare have changed a great deal in the last twenty-five years. If we have to come to grips with an enemy-there is one enemy in our minds-the thing that would determine our success would be the large manufacturing and industrial capacity of Canada and the United States. If the war followed the pattern of the last war, in which we bombed the Ruhr valley which contains the manufacturing centres for war materials for

Germany, it would naturally follow that our enemy would bomb our industrial areas and the industrial areas of the great country to the south. That is something to be considered, because the bombing of those areas has become part of warfare as it exists at the present time.
We are striving, and other nations are striving, to put industries which manufacture war materials, such as guns, aeroplanes and that type of thing, out of business. For that reason, I believe it would be a possibility that this country and the country to the south of us would be bombed. For that reason I feel that, even as the hon. member who just spoke, while a great deal of the work done in such an emergency would be voluntary, yet there is an onus on the government to build up a very elaborate plan for the defence of this country. The same thing happened in England during the last war. During the bombing of the industrial areas the civilian population suffered, and suffered severely. Practically one-third of the houses were destroyed at that time, along with the casualties which existed at that time. The same condition could exist in Canada. I do not like that note in the minister's address in which he intimated that we are more or less going to take a chance. We are not going to build up an organization that is going to rust. Mr. Chairman, I do not believe the time will ever come when we should take a chance on this country or the people who live in it.

Supply-National Defence about hose couplings. There is no reason why the same type of hose couplings could not be in common use across Canada. We have had disasters in Canada before. In the last year we had to deal with one in the Fraser valley; we had a flood in Winnipeg, and we had the terrible fires in Quebec. Those things are happening and causing a great deal of suffering. This agency would not be allowed to rust in disuse because of the things I have cited that have happened in the last year or two. They may happen again in the future.
So far as the training of people in the care of casualties is concerned, that is not something that is going to rust. If the lessons in the care of casualties and first aid are well learned, people are not going to forget them. They can be of use at any time. The stockpiling of medical supplies and food are things that can be used at any time. The hon. member who has just spoken mentioned the possibility of hospitals being bombed. That shows us that arrangements should be made outside those areas to take care of casualties, because the hospital is just as apt to be destroyed as any other place. In his reply, I would ask the minister-after all he is at the head of this organization and it is a difficult assignment, but I am going to ask him these questions-to indicate what arrangements have been made in the matter of an air raid warning across Canada.
Let us suppose that by means of radar we are warned of the approach of enemy planes. Is there one warning that will be spread all across Canada? So far as sirens are concerned, I wonder how many municipalities in Canada have sirens that could warn the people? Some days ago we heard some noise from a new siren on the Hunter building. Then, this morning, I read in the newspaper that we are going to do some excavating and dig down about two floors below the parliament buildings to have some protection. Possibly there are some members who would like to crawl into such a hole during these debates. But this matter is not going ahead, and if this emergency should occur at the present time we are still taking chances. Will the minister tell us what has been done by way of keeping the water and food supply in Canada free from contamination. Are the large reservoirs of the cities protected? I doubt if any municipality in Canada is mounting a guard or taking any steps to maintain a proper water supply for the people.
As of now, how many of our people have been trained in chemical and germ warfare? Has this matter been brought before the people by means of booklets or pamphlets,

Supply-National Defence telling them that something like this could happen? The average person feels that this is something one reads about. In looking at this whole picture, they feel that it cannot happen here. We are only talking about this. I wonder what surveys have been made in Canada for bomb shelters. I wonder how far the training has advanced in all the cities and towns of Canada where there are possible targets. How far has the training of people in the care of casualties advanced?
I ask the minister what has been done about stockpiling food and medical supplies, and whether these supplies have been placed in areas outside the large cities where they could be reached in the event of the city being bombed. Lastly I ask the minister this question: How far have we gone into the possibility of fire either from bombs or from fifth columnists? Certainly the fire brigades of every town or organized municipality in the country should be receiving training along that line. As p,art of their training the municipalities might like to have their own air wardens or their own fire wardens, apart from their fire system, because, as you will realize, in a city even the size of Ottawa, the present fire brigade would find it difficult to control the whole community.
In the last war in England they set up fire wardens who took charge of certain areas, and they had fire watchers. It was a good organization. These people stayed on; they worked for weeks, months and years. But I again come back to the minister's statement of last night which, while he has corrected the statement that I made, did smack somehow of a feeling that, well, we will take a chance. We are going to have to take a chance; there is no way out of it. We will just have to do the best we can.
It may be that out of the asking for more money in this debate today for civil defence nothing will happen, but I would like to believe that the minister, or any member of the government, if nothing happens in the next three years, will not say: There now, we knew there was no occasion to spend this money. We, your wise government, did not spend this money and inflict taxes on you because we felt nothing was going to happen.
I ask the minister now: Does he honestly feel that nothing can happen? If it could happen, why cannot we be prepared and fully prepared? The amount of $5 million that we are spending is only a drop in the bucket in comparison with the $5 billion we are spending for defence. Therefore I think the minister finds himself in the position


where he feels that he would like to do a great deal more than is being done.
I do realize it is difficult to establish an organization across Canada which would be adequate for the protection of this country. No doubt the size of the country and the population make the matter of civil defence a difficult question to deal with. But even with that, we have certain cities in certain parts of the country which would be vulnerable targets in the event of an attack such as has been visualized by some hon. members since the debate started.
Therefore in closing I feel that even if these things that we are doing for our protection-and I include the lot from air raid shelters to the training of civilians-even if these are never used, we should still go ahead and protect the people of this country, and, so far as the training is concerned, ensure protection against fire. That brings up the matter of hose couplings which has occupied a great deal of the time of the house. They could all be used at any time. Having suffered from disasters, three or four in the past year or two, we could still with advantage use the set-up for civilian defence in the time of an emergency, even if there were no enemy attacks.
Again I cannot help comparing the small amount set up for civil defence of this country with the total expenditure on defence, and drawing the minister's attention to the fact that in war as it exists at the present time, and looking back at the first war. civilians suffer, and they sometimes have been in more danger than the people in the army. It is part of present-day warfare; it is part of the strategy of the enemy air force.
This matter brought on, both last night and today, a debate in which I am glad to say a number of members were interested. But I say to the minister that the advice of the members and their feelings in this matter are expressed in an attempt to safeguard the people of this country and to help them in the event of a tragedy of this type coming to pass.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks in connection with this debate will be very brief. I am inclined to agree with the speech made by the hon. member for Red Deer yesterday who said that in his opinion, in dealing with these defence estimates, the house had wasted practically four days. In that connection I have noticed that our friends in the C.C.F. party have not spoken in this debate, and I am presuming that they are more or less in accord with

government policy. There has been very little criticism from the Sociil Credit group; but we find the grand old Conservative party going to bat in connection with this debate, and we also find them not in agreement. The aged member for Nanaimo apparently has disagreed-
Oh, oh.
He has been in the house a long time, and he disagrees with the more youthful member from the other seat in British Columbia. They have disagreed on procedure. We find today-
On a question of privilege, there has been no disagreement between myself and any other member, and I am not so very old, after all is said and done.
Well, the record of the house speaks for itself.
He looks younger than you do.
Order.
On a question of privilege, I merely want to confirm the hon. member for Nanaimo in both particulars.
Well, Hansard will speak for itself. If these two gentlemen were in agreement then a great misuse has been made of the English language.
By you.

Thus we find today again that while the hon. member for Calgary East said yesterday that in all fairness to the government in the last year or so considerable progress had been made in the matter of defence, yet we find the hon. member for Lake Centre today saying that little had been accomplished since the year 1948.
One is a soldier.
One is a soldier, that is correct.

On a question of privilege, the hon. member for Yorkton should consult Hansard again and keep his records straight. I was speaking yesterday on certain things that had been done in the army, navy and air force. The hon. member for Lake Centre was speaking of civil defence entirely. They are two different things.
You are all balled up.

That is all right. Apparently my hon. friends in the official opposition are getting balled up and are getting excited now, and even the young soldier who has just joined the house is getting impatient. I say that my friends of
Supply-National Defence the official opposition ought to get more coordination. I have stressed that all along. They have disagreed on procedure; they have disagreed on whether the government is doing a good job or not.
No; there is complete agreement on that.
Let me make this prophecy. I have exhorted them in this house previously to try to get together and get a little co-ordination in their affairs, or they may not even be the official opposition.
We are co-ordinated; your thoughts are not.

I think I am correct in saying that the official opposition has successfully wasted at least three days in talking on procedure in this house. I quite agree with the hon. member from the Social Credit ranks who said that Stalin himself would have enjoyed the performance put on by the official opposition in this house in the last few days. The inference today again, as it was last night, was that the government was not spending enough on civilian defence. We have before us billions being spent on defence generally, and very little if any criticism has been offered by the official opposition in -connection with that expenditure. Thus far they have argued chiefly about procedure.
Are we to take it for granted that they are satisfied with the main estimates for this department? They imply that, because of the vote for home defence, the government is taking a chance, that it is not going far enough, and that it is not spending enough. Well, I would point out that in connection with home defence the total amount is not being spent by the federal government. One must always take into consideration the amount being spent by municipal and provincial governments.
Anyone who has followed the procedure in connection with bombing and air attacks knows that the best defence for Canada is on our northern boundaries. He must also know that that defence is being looked after by the Department of National Defence. One of our greatest expenditures is for that purpose. He should also know that a country, even one as intelligent as Russia, is not going to bomb small communities throughout the Dominion of Canada. If they did get through our defence of radar and our aircraft in the north country, they would not do that. That is only common sense. Certain targets will be picked out in the most strategic centres in Canada and the United States, if Russia happens to be our enemy. For instance it is idle for the leader of the Social Credit

Supply-National Defence group to suggest that our people should flee to the barns, and establish their homes there. I do not think any intelligent nation would bother bombing ninety per cent of the farms in Canada, even if they could get across our boundary. They are not going to fly from Russia in their large bombers, and waste atom bombs on cities such as the city of Yorkton, or such places. They will pick out certain strategic points of military value. I doubt even if they would bother with the city of Ottawa.
The chief defences should be in those places of military value, and should not be wasted. I was down to California again last winter. Down there they have a population of about eight million people congested in a small area. Those are the places where-
Mr. Chairman-

You make your speech, buttercup, later on. You are up all the time; now give somebody else a chance.
Any nation of intelligence-and the Russians have some intelligence-will pick out those centres of heavy population and strategic military value. They are not going to waste bombs on small communities throughout Canada. There is no reason, of course, why those communities should not have firefighting equipment; but it is idle for anyone to urge that the government and the department should spend money in every community of Canada to build dugouts, concrete shelters and everything else for the protection of those people.
If Russian planes did get through they would pick out strategic points in Canada- and I believe the government of this country has intelligence enough to have picked out those points, and to have arranged for their protection, to see that those points are amply protected.
But the idea of spending millions upon millions of dollars in the defence of towns and villages that have no more chance of being attacked than the man in the moon is just a waste of money. Further, those members who advocate such a thing are unnecessarily exciting the people. In two wars we lost 100,000 in killed, and if another war comes it will be a total war in which civilians as well as others will be attacked, and will be in the same position as the reserve troops. While we do not want a war, it might have the healthy effect throughout the dominion of uniting the people a little more closely together than they have been in the past, through equal suffering.
No one in Canada should get the idea that he or she will be free of trouble if another war breaks out. But, as for the spending


of more money on shelters, and all that sort of thing, I say the government would be well advised to pick out the strategic points first and to make sure that they are protected. The government is well advised to spend money on our northern defences, and all that sort of thing, to keep the enemy out of the air.
I do not think the small points in Canada need worry much about having large bombs dropped on them, nor do they need to follow the suggestion of the leader of the Social Credit party, and flee to their barns. I do not think that will be necessary.
As I said at the outset, I did not intend to take up much time.
Oh no.

My young friend, the young soldier of the last war, is very good at interrupting. If he has a question to ask, then let him get up on his hind legs and ask it.
The official opposition have complimented the government upon the selection of General Worthington. We have a good man at the head of civil defence, a man who has been across the Dominion of Canada. I am sure that in my province of Saskatchewan he will receive splendid co-operation in every city.
