speechtext: That is right.

They are not stampeded, at all. I think members generally from the west, in all parties, are not receiving protests from their cities-at least they have not said so in the house. Even Rome was not built in a day. The fact that there are not complaints from the larger urban municipalities in the western provinces shows that the people are reasonably well satisfied with what is being done, and are reasonably satisfied with the contribution they are making. They are not complaining about what the federal government is or is not doing in the matter of civil defence.
As I said earlier, the best civilian defence is military defence through our air force and our navy, and the troops we are training. That is the best defence we could have. If it comes to a total war, we will all be in it, in any event-and I would repeat that that might do more to mould Canada than anything we have seen in the efforts of the official opposition in the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to open my mouth this afternoon; but following the speech of the hon. member for Yorkton I am wondering whether we should not ask the director of civil defence to have a squad here, to take care of us.

This matter of civil defence is serious. The minister has been stressing that point constantly, and I think hon. members agree as to its seriousness. My understanding is that this debate started last night only. It has not yet gone on a full day. Why hon. members suggest there has been delay and waste of time in this important matter I, for one, do not understand.
There may be some reason for the hon. member's indulging in personalities, and in describing people as being youthful or aged -but what that has to do with an important subject of this kind, I cannot see. I think if the hon. member were to look into his speech he would realize, upon reflection, that this whole matter of civil defence is one requiring the most careful consideration of people throughout the country. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard said this afternoon, it is as important to each member as it is to the government. Surely that is consistent, is it not?
I would not think it proper to indulge in the kind of personalities and the type of discussion we have been having. The official opposition may be hamstrung in numbers, but it is trying to do its job as best it can. If it believes this is the way in which we should proceed, then surely it ought not to be criticized as it has been criticized this afternoon. This is an important subject-and 1 leave it at that.
I have risen to ask the minister one or two questions. He has had discussions with the provinces, and plans have been worked out. I am speaking only for the province of Newfoundland. A director of civil defence was appointed for Newfoundland, but he resigned some three months ago and no one has been appointed in his place. I do not know what has happened and I do not believe anyone else does.
I do not think we need to enter into the realms of imagination to consider Newfoundland as being strategically important. There are United States bases and airports located there, and it is important in operating a convoy system. But we do not know what is happening. The answer may be that which was given by the hon. member for Lake Centre, that it is a question of finance. Perhaps the province has not the money to take care of these matters. I submit that the minister should make a full explanation this afternoon and tell us what has been done in Newfoundland.
There has been nothing in the newspapers in the past month to indicate what has been done. The minister may be able to explain. I feel like the hon. member for Lake Centre,
Supply-National Defence and with all due respect to some of the previous speakers, this is something in connection with which the government should give full direction and I think also that the great bulk of the money should come from the government.

Mr. Chairman, I hope that the hon. member for Yorkton and other Liberals who may hear members of the opposition making suggestions to the minister or criticizing what the minister has been doing will not take us to task and introduce into this discussion petty party politics. Personally I think that this matter is of too great concern to the people of Canada for a minister or any government supporter to place any criticism offered on a party political basis.
I am not in agreement with the hon. member for Yorkton when he says that the people of Canada are reasonably satisfied with what has been done in the matter of civil defence because no complaints have been registered with the minister. He indicates that if they were not satisfied complaints would be pouring in to the minister. I think the people of Canada just are not civil defence conscious at the present time. They are not turning their minds to civil defence.
As one hon. member has stated already, we hate to think of ourselves being in the midst of war. We hate to think of war coming to this country. It is difficult for the people of Canada to realize such a possibility and as a result very little thought is given by the ordinary citizen to the matter of civil defence.
I agree with the minister that civil defence is primarily a co-operative and volunteer effort on the part of the body of Canadian citizens. I realize that the essence of the job is education. It is not just a matter of spending money; it is not merely a matter of buying equipment or providing it for the provinces and municipalities; it is a matter of teaching the Canadian people what to do under certain circumstances and what precautions to take. It represents one of the biggest jobs that any government has to do.
I feel that that job cannot be done without a nucleus of full-time personnel, not only in each province but in each county or township or area of the provinces. If an effective job is to be carried out by volunteer workers there must be a core of full-time, well-trained people to give direction and leadership to those who are ready to volunteer their services and to assist in getting these ideas across to the people as a whole.
I presume the minister has given some thought to the contrast between the amount provided in the estimates for civil defence and what is provided for the other branches

Supply-National Defence of national defence. I understand the estimates provide $5 million for civil defence, but we find that $8,621,000 has been allocated in the national defence estimates for professional and special services. That is much more than is allocated for civil defence purposes. The minister's department and the provincial departments will require a considerable number of personnel well-trained, full-time-at least for a while-if anything is to be achieved in the realm of civil defence.
Has the minister any information of what preparations have been made by the various provinces for civil defence? Has he any information regarding the number of permanent or full-time employees engaged by the provincial governments in civil defence work? Has he any knowledge of how many people have been trained to date in the special courses and who could give leadership in this field?
About 450.
With that information we would have some idea of the over-all picture of just what the provinces, the municipalities and the federal government are doing.

When the minister replies I should like him to deal, in so far as he can without breaching any security provisions, with what progress has been made in providing for early warning by the armed forces to the civil defence authorities in the event of enemy attack. When the minister made his statement on May 11 he described the priority in that regard and stated that it was the duty of the military to provide the means of receiving warning through radar and other devices which have been referred to, that they would also have the duty of warning the civil defence authorities, whose duty it would be to alert the various localities which were expected to be the targets of that particular raid. It seems to me that that is one of the most important things in this whole matter. I refer to the details for receiving early warning. I should be glad if the minister could tell us about that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the time has now come for me to deal with a number of the questions that have been raised. May I say this-and I say this in full appreciation of the value of the discussion, which I think has been useful-if any hon. member thinks that I have taken to heart personally anything that has been said., I am sure that hon. member does not know me.
I really think this has been a most useful debate because this is an extremely important matter and it is by no means an easy one to deal with.


I know that the hon. member for Lanark would not want to misinterpret what I said when I used the words "take a calculated risk". But I feel that one in government and holding this particular post at this time must be courageously frank and not give the impression that it would be possible to provide a complete civil defence for this country. That cannot be done in any country. All we can hope to do-in the light of the appraisal of the situation as given to us by military authorities-in co-operation with other jurisdictions of government, is to build up the best and most effective civil defence organization that is possible, and to do that without in any way prejudicing the primary effort that must now occupy every free country in the free world, recognizing that if war should come it can be won only by giving first support to the armed forces of the nation. That effort necessitates that we do not provide for a needless diversion of energy or of resources. I know that everyone in this committee will agree with that statement. That is the sort of thing I had in mind when I was speaking.
If the hon. member for York South who has just spoken will permit me to say so, I think he made a good speech. I say that not because he agreed with what I said-although I suppose I am somewhat encouraged to so appraise his effort because he has spoken as he did-but because I believe that what he said is surely what we all really believe, namely, that this business of civil defence is essentially one of mutual aid.
If there is one field in which I admit without any hesitation that I am not fully satisfied by any means, it is the field of education. I believe that the municipalities, the provinces and ourselves will have to accelerate the techniques we have for bringing home to the people the important facts involved in civil defence. I say that frankly without depreciating what has already been done and without underestimating the value of plans which we have in that very connection. There are in our own services in Ottawa, and also in those of at least nine provincial governments, individuals who are devoting their full time to the job of trying to find the most effective way of bringing home to the individual citizen-the boy and the girl in the school, the teacher, the worker in the factory, all of us-those methods that can most effectively be employed in the event of the kind of disaster which could happen but which none of us wants to happen.
I must say that the speech delivered by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard had this suggestion with which I know we will

all agree, namely, that each of us has a responsibility. We are members of parliament and we can do a great deal to bring home to the people a proper appreciation of this problem, without creating panic or fear, by letting them know that it is only good common sense to develop certain techniques in this matter of civil defence.
I believe that the statement I made the other night possibly has been forgotten in the present discussion. If hon. members will do me the honour of referring to it, they will see there a statement of principles which I believe will find ready acceptance by most people in this country and by most hon. members of the House of Commons. There was a frank recognition of the fact that at the centre you cannot do this job completely, that the primary responsibility must rest at the local level and therefore the primary influence must be voluntary effort based on the principle of mutual aid.
The hon. member for Peace River made an excellent suggestion, namely that each home was the place where civil defence should begin. I think he used the words "domestic granary". That was the basis of Britain's civil defence scheme during the last war. Sir John Hodsoll told me in Washington the other day when we were discussing this matter-Sir John Hodsoll being the director of civil defence in the United Kingdom- that the people of the United- Kingdom were able to deal with air raids more successfully than were the people of Hamburg for that very reason. While some of them took to the tubes, the vast majority of the people of the United Kingdom showed defiance and used their own homes as the centre. That is an experience that I think we might well bear in mind in considering the matter of shelter, whether it be communal or private, or whatever may be the scheme devised. It is not without significance that at the present time His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom-and I use the United Kingdom as an example not because we must emulate some other country but because of their experience and because of their proximity to attack-are not at the present time engaging in any expenditure on shelters.
I believe that if we will look at our own situation in the light of the character of our country, we shall find that we have three levels of government: the federal, the provincial and the municipal. The ten provincial governments and ourselves have agreed as to what should be done. While hon. members here may criticize-and may properly do so from their point of view-what we have done, I can only say that what we are doing is the result of agreement of those in the ten
Supply-National Defence provincial governments who have jurisdictional influence over the local government in each of those ten provinces. I have given a statement of what we have done, and have told of the various committees that we have set up and that are working, such as the transportation committee, the medical committee, the welfare committee, the telecommunications committee and so on, and the responsibility for the training of instructors to carry on the work of civil defence in the community. I have told the house all about that.
I hold in my hand a report given to me by each of the ten provincial governments of our country. Each province has designated one of its ministers as the minister of civil defence. Each minister has built up an organization on the provincial level corresponding in many particulars to the organization that we have at the national level, and in turn has stimulated action in the various municipalities. As I said last evening there is not more than one city of 50,000 or over which does not have its own civil defence director. That is the first thing for a community to do. That director, paid by the municipality in every case, is the centre around which is built the local organization.
At one time in our discussions with the Red Cross and St. John Ambulance they wanted to work, particularly the Red Cross, as a national disaster organization. We took the position, with which the provinces agreed, that the Red Cross and other national organizations should act in co-ordination with the plans of the locality. As a result the Red Cross in my own city of Windsor, for example, does not operate as part of a national body but is integrated into the local scheme. That is a very important matter, for if an attack should occur it is not what may be done in any central capital that is going to count; it is what can be done in the particular municipality where the job has to be carried out. The effectiveness of that kind of mutual aid will depend upon the kind of direction the local civil defence director has been able to give in enlisting the support of the people of that community.
Those are basic considerations that so far in this debate have been overlooked. In Montreal, one of the important cities of our country, Brigadier Gauvreau, a distinguished soldier of the last war, has been appointed civil defence director, and he has done an excellent job in the short time he has been at work. I mention the city of Montreal simply to indicate that many hon. members have failed to appreciate the tremendous amount of work that is being done; and that work was begun in the first instance as a

Supply-National Defence result of the stimulation by the present civil defence co-ordinator in Canada, General Worthington. In Montreal, wardens and other civil defence personnel, working on a voluntary basis, have been and are being enlisted. The other day they had a meeting at which several thousand were in attendance; and that work is going on, along with the contribution being made by welfare organizations, medical bodies and others. The doctors themselves are now holding special clinics and preparing for the problems that may have to be met.
Then in the city of Sault Ste. Marie the other day on both sides of the border exercises were held in anticipation of a possible air raid. Thousands of individuals, including nurses, doctors, welfare workers, St. John Ambulance personnel and Red Cross members took part in those exercises. A similar exercise on a more modest scale took place not long ago in Detroit and in Windsor, where I am happy to say one of the best civil defence organizations is being developed under a director who had extensive training in the United Kingdom during the last war.
I mention these cities not because I prefer them to others but simply to indicate the work that is going on. I do not say it is perfect. I know there is a great deal yet to do. 1 will not be satisfied until this job is done and the danger is past; but on the other hand I do not want anyone to underestimate the work already carried out at the provincial and municipal levels. I have before me a report from British Columbia, for instance. I do not want to go into all the details, but there they have an organization composed of representatives of health and welfare organizations, the army, voluntary organizations, industry and all the other groups in a community upon which one would have to rely in a situation such as this. The hon. member for Lake Centre spoke of the agreements that have been made between state and state in the United States. Well, long before the United States thought of that this country had achieved and completed such agreements. Here, for instance, is a report on the nature of the agreement between Alberta and British Columbia, which also shows the extent of the preparations that have been made in British Columbia, the courses being given, the training being carried on, the schools being set up and the instructors being provided. The report deals with the activities of the civil defence director in circulating civil defence bulletins all through British Columbia in an endeavour to keep up interest in civil defence work, and so on.
[Mr. Martin.!

I could go on. I have here the report of the province of Alberta, of which I have given some indication already in reply to the hon. member for Bow River. I note here, for instance, that in connection with publicity and education Mr. Gerhart inaugurated a series of broadcasts early in January, which is still continuing and which is carried over most of the Alberta stations. They are doing everything they can to bring home to the people some of the elementary facts of this program. I want to give fair warning now that we have plans at the national level for a heavy educational program. That is likely to cost a great deal of money, and I would hope that no hon. member who today is criticizing our lack of educational effort will rise in his place next year, when I bring in a report of the expenditure through our information service in the Department of National Health and Welfare, and protest the amount we have spent in carrying on work to supplement that being done by the provinces.
As long as you keep it separate.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
My hon. friend says as long as I do something. I know I will not be able to do anything that will completely satisfy my esteemed and hon. friend. Here is the province of Saskatchewan, which has a civil defence training school. Someone may ask why Saskatchewan should worry about the possibility of air attack, since it would not be regarded as a primary target. That may be so, but it is a very important reception centre. From our experience in the flood disaster in Manitoba we know how essential it proved to be to have machinery in Saskatchewan for the reception of thousands of hospital patients, numbers of old people and others who found refuge there. The experience of those days is being used in building up a very effective civil defence organization there, as in other places,
As to the province of Ontario, as I said last evening, only last Friday I had a long discussion with the minister in charge of civil defence matters, Mr. Welsh. Every community in Ontario of major size has a civil defence director-with the exception of the city of Ottawa-and Mr. Welsh wrote me yesterday saying he had written the authorities in Ottawa asking them to emulate in that particular the example of every other community of any consequence in this province. With that single exception, every community of any significance in Ontario has its own organization. The plan in Ontario is to have the organization on a county unit basis, to have the major community in the

county serve as the centre. That direction was given by Mr. Welsh about two weeks ago, and as a result a considerable acceleration in organization has taken place already. The other day in London I was talking to Colonel Eric Harris, the civil defence director for that city. He outlined for General Worthington and myself the whole plan not only for the organization of the county but for the organization of that whole district, covering some eight or nine counties. So that while one can only give here a general picture of what is being done in each of the provinces, one can see that in the province of Ontario, too, a very considerable amount of organization is under way. The Ontario government has not yet appointed its civil defence coordinator, but Mr. Welsh has been extremely active in formulating plans for his province.
In the province of Quebec a school began operations today. There, too, the municipalities have appointed their civil defence directors, and direction is being given to them by myself and my department in conjunction with the co-operative arrangement that we have with the provinces. Similarly in the province of New Brunswick. Incidentally, we have trained eleven civil defence officials for the province of New Brunswick, and they have now returned to their province to take positions of leadership in the direction of the civil defence program. The same is true of Nova Scotia. In Nova Scotia one of the significant things is the prominent part being taken by women in giving leadership in the building up of all local civil defence organizations.
I have just mentioned these provinces, and for the sake of a complete reference I would not want to leave out the province of Prince Edward Island, where a total of four civil defence officials have received training at federal expense. They are now giving leadership in various civil defence activities in that province. The province of Newfoundland has its civil defence provincial committee under the chairmanship of Mr. Curtis. Five civil defence officials who were trained in our school are assisting him in the planning of the work for the whole province. So, when one comes to make an assessment of what is being done in this field in Canada, one must see not only what is being done in Ottawa under federal direction but also what is being done under municipal and provincial direction.
The result is we are building an organization for civil defence which I feel, in the light of all the circumstances, represents if not the most complete, at any rate a commendable effort. The time to look for completion of achievement is after the danger
Supply-National Defence has passed. Before I take my seat, I should note that the hon. member for Lanark referred to stockpiling. I have already dealt with that. I have told him of our plans to stockpile medical supplies at strategic centres, for which arrangements have been made in conjunction with the Department of National Defence. As I said the other night, I agree with him about the importance of encouraging the greatest amount of first aid training. We have made special arrangements with the St. John Ambulance Corps for that purpose; that is something we must do whether we accelerate our program or not. I agree fully with him that that is a useful kind of training, and will always be of great benefit to this country.
We hope to be able, through schools, service clubs and church organizations, primarily under the direction of the St. John Ambulance, to carry on an increasing amount of first aid training all over this country. It is something that will serve us in good stead in the days of peace, in the days of twilight between peace and war, or in the days of war itself. I can assure the hon. member for Lanark there will be no relaxation of that effort. I have already explained what we are doing about defence against ABC warfare. The school we have at Connaught Ranges, which some of us are going to visit between six o'clock and adjournment tonight, is the school which is dealing with that as well as with other matters. I want to say, therefore, to the hon, member for Lanark that he can be assured that no effort in the important field of medical and welfare endeavour is going to be overlooked. If what has been done to date does not fully satisfy him, that may be because a full appreciation of what has been done has not been given. But I can assure him that the fullest contact exists with our nursing association, with the Canadian Medical Association, and all those bodies upon whom we have to depend-the men who will stimulate action, not at Ottawa nor in Toronto nor in any one of our capitals, but on the part of the health workers in the village or town concerned where the civil defence organization is being built up.
Now, we are proceeding with this as wisely and as energetically as we know how. We are not looking for commendation as to whether our achievement is worthy of praise. I am saying that no effort is being lost to develop an effective organization. If it is effective, we are not looking for praise. That will be due to the collaboration we are receiving from every one of the ten provincial governments of Canada who are in full

The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Robinson for the second reading of Bill No. 118, to incorporate Border Pipeline Corporation, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Herridge.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment that has been moved on this bill. The amendment seeks to have this pipe line follow an all-Canadian route. I am not opposed to the company.
I am not opposed to the personnel of the company. I do not know the officers concerned. I am concerned, however, about this pipe line bill not including a section to the effect that the pipe line will be built through Canadian territory. So far as I can see, and I am satisfied now after investigating the point, there is no physical reason why the pipe line could not be built through Canadian territory much cheaper than through United States territory. There is ample evidence to prove that point. Today I believe the issue is merely financial interests versus Canadian interests. By "Canadian interests" I mean the general welfare of the Canadian people which is involved in getting this pipe line to serve our country first.
Unfortunately this bill will be passed in spite of all the arguments that we can put up against it, because the government majority will put it through. This bill, like all the bills concerned with taking gas to the coast, has met with the same objections from the provincial government of British Columbia, city councils, boards of trade, chambers of commerce, and all the bodies within that province who are opposed to the passing of this bill without the particular clause I mentioned. I believe the government should now assume its right to direct the flow of our natural resources along lines that will give Canadians as a whole the greatest benefit.
Sending our gas and oil to the United States, as we are proposing to do under this bill, does not indicate a sound policy on the part of the government, if the government is

going to try to build Canada first. We can easily understand why the United States wants our gas and oil. They have exploited their own to the full, and the resources in California are now petering out, as is well known to everyone. According to a statement made by the American gas association, the natural gas industry in the United States is finding that new discoveries are not keeping pace with production. The ratio of reserves to production in the United States, according to the American gas association, has dropped from 32-49 in 1949 to 26-17 in 1950. They are taking steps to conserve the remaining supply. In the meantime, their policy obviously is to import all they can from Canada, and thereby deplete our resources as well as their own. Unfortunately, Canada has not a sound national policy for the conservation of our gas and oil. At least, I do not feel that we have. We may well find our own supplies exhausted in a very few years' time.
I believe that the conservation of resources is a moral obligation upon all members of parliament, and on the government. We must assume that obligation not only for the protection of our generation but in the interests of generations of Canadians who will occupy this land when we are gone. I am not opposed to any surplus gas being sold to the United States. I think they are entitled to it, but only when it is surplus and after it has supplied Canadian needs.
I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

I had a few specific
questions that I wished to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Mention was made on numerous occasions today and last night about hose couplings. The minister told us that something in the neighbourhood of $977,500 is going to be spent on fire-fighting equipment, chiefly these hose couplings. The thing we have not found out, and which I should like to know, is whether any decision has been made on a standardized coupling.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the decision, of course, does not rest with us. There are a number of different plans, and of course the objective is to bring them all into a common system. The fire chiefs have had a meeting, both on the national and on the provincial level, discussing this very matter. They have not finalized their decisions.
The business of standardizing hose couplings of course is not only a civil defence matter, but of permanent all-time value, as my hon. friend will appreciate. However, the government has thought it desirable that we should endeavour not to wait until there is full national accord. It was for that reason that we did make a tentative arrangement, subject to plans being submitted and approved by the province of Ontario, in the discussion that I referred to that was held with Colonel Welsh last week; and he has taken steps to bring about such uniformity and standardization in the province of Ontario. It is hoped that as a result of that action uniformity may be stimulated elsewhere.

If I understood the minister correctly, they are proceeding on a provincial basis, in the first place as far as Ontario is concerned, in the hope that the standardized coupling adapted for use throughout Ontario will then be adopted throughout the rest of Canada. Do I understand by that that the only province in which any money has been advanced to aid in the standardization of these couplings is Ontario, and that it will be the only one in which they have agreed on some standard?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No. The arrangement that we have made with the province is that we would pay one-third toward the cost of these hose couplings. The offer applies of course to all provinces.

The point I am getting at is that apparently no agreement has yet been made that this standardized coupling be used. So far, the only thing that is being done in

Supply-National Defence a practical way is this grant to Ontario to standardize its couplings. That is correct, is it?
Yes.

What steps is the minister taking in his position as being in charge of civil defence for the dominion to get the other provinces to agree to take this same standard coupling? In the event that they do not take it, what is to be the result? It would seem to me that this is a matter of such importance that the dominion government should ensure by some means or other that general agreement is reached on the part of all the provinces before any of the money is put out. I do not know, but ^ it would seem to me that would be the wise course.

My hon. friend may be certain that everything that we can do to get uniformity will be done, but we cannot force municipalities or provinces to do anything contrary to their will. The most effective means, of course, is the one of persuasion, and that is what we are engaged in. The practice I have followed in the case of Ontario is being followed with every other province. As a matter of fact, I had some discussion today with another government in connection with the same matter.
I want to ask the minister a Question. From what he said a moment ago I assumed that the intention of the department is complete national standardization. Is that correct?

Standardization of hose
couplings.

Any attempt to do that is impracticable, is it not? For example, there are many different types and sizes of hydrants, and the hose coupling that you may perfect for the province of Ontario may not at the hydrant in any of the other provinces. Is it not the logical thing to do to make a a survey of a province, determine the type of hydrant used in that province and perfect the coupling that can be used and standardized as between municipalities in that province?

That is what is being
attempted.

I do not think that complete
uniformity or standardization in this country on a national basis is possible. I do not see where there is any possibility of using the equipment, or the fire-fighting machinery, from the province of Ontario in the province of British Columbia or in the province of Nova Scotia. I think the thing to do-and

perhaps the minister's officials are doing it-is to get a complete provincial survey of the type of hydrant and the size of hydrant and manufacture for that province the type of equipment that is adapted to the hydrants in that province, because you need standardization as between one municipality and the other.
I do not see anything happening in any province where it might be necessary to move in fire-fighting equipment from another province. Complete standardization was possible in Britain because they had a unified set-up to start with. Because of the distances that exist in this country the local unit is the place to start the survey on a provincial scale.
Over a year ago I listened to the fire marshal of Nova Scotia address a banquet, and at that time I was led to believe that there was almost complete uniformity and stardardization in that province. Rather than taking it on a national scale and deciding that Ontario is going to be the focal point, perfecting equipment that might suit in this province and then saying that you must get uniformity in the sixty or seventy different types of hydrants throughout the country, a start should be made in one province. After all, the hydrant is the key in the thing.
I wanted to say that because I got the impression from the minister that they were going to take Ontario as an example, and from the ivory tower in Ottawa say to the provinces that they have to re-equip to suit the type of coupling that we are going to have in this province. I just thought I would leave these thoughts with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We do not disagree on that.
I do not know too much about this matter of hose couplings, but my understanding is that you can get an adapter which you can use on any hydrant.
You cannot do that.

The hose can be put on by means of that adapter. Whether that is correct, I am not sure, but that is my understanding.
One of the difficulties in this thing of not having the same equipment throughout the whole of the dominion is that every province except Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island abuts onto some other province and you are very likely to have help going from one to the other.
Another matter that I wish to ask about is the item that was mentioned, namely, radiation detection instruments, for which $962,000 is to be spent this year, with an additional

$50,000 being ordered to be paid for next year. Can the minister tell us what these radiation detection instruments are, and whether it is intended by means of this vote, or subsequent votes of this kind, to equip all of the municipalities with these instruments?

To answer the latter part of my hon. friend's question, we will naturally provide the equipment in those areas where we believe, in the light of the assessment that is made, there is a prior necessity, and we will *proceed on that basis. Obviously, it would be impossible, when you have not got unlimited quantities, to try and supply them to all communities. However, we are saying that in these places where we believe the need in terms of priority is greatest we will supply them.

The minister did not say what sort of detection equipment this was. It was also part of my question. In view of what the minister has said I should like to ask another question. Is the dominion government paying the entire cost of this detection equipment, or is it on a one-third basis, the same as the hose couplings?
The present agreement is that we shall supply these.
What kind of equipment is it?
What does my hon. friend mean by the question? There are many kinds of equipment.
Are these geiger counters.

These are first of all to try to ascertain the existence of radioactivity. Also there are supplementary auxiliary units of use in the medical field, which, where there is radioactivity, are applied to the human body, and yield positive, negative, minor or major results.

The next item comprises a
series of things, and refers to sirens, to the extent of $252,000. Is the dominion government supplying sirens to all municipalities, or is this on a one-third basis?

training equipment, and mention of pamphlets. In addition to pamphlets, what does

Rescue sets. Then, of course, pamphlets have a primary purpose of serving in an educational program. However, there will be pamphlets not intended merely for public education, but to help in connection with specific things such as a greater measure of first-aid training, and to encourage some phases of home nursing. The other type of pamphlet will be designed to bring home to the general public the kinds of protections which, in the light of experience in heavily bombed-out areas such as those in the United Kingdom, and in areas such as Nagasaki and Hiroshima, are thought to be the protective measures which should be taken.
Some of that information is now out in various ways. Some comes through in the form of films, some in the form of radio talks and dramatizations. It is done most effectively through films. As I said last night, we have arranged for the use of films produced in the United States, and we hope also to be able to get two films from Great Britain. It may be necessary to make some readaptations for our own local use.
Then the stretchers about which I spoke last night are the stretchers we are providing for the school in Ottawa, the school in Saskatchewan, in Montreal, and so on.

Possibly the minister did
not understand my question. I asked what this training equipment is, apart from the pamphlets, the stretchers and the films which are mentioned specifically.

I shall have to send for the

Referring to the early warning system, the minister said before six o'clock that national defence military personnel would receive the first warning of the approach of enemy aircraft, that they would send that information to civil defence *centres which, in turn, would be responsible for sending it from the centres to the various municipalities and other civil defence subcentres so that the whole civil defence scheme might be alerted.

speechtext: From the time the warning is given to the defence communication centre, where there will be civil defence personnel in 24-hour attendance, consideration is now being given to separate schemes that will provide for a special communications system.
