speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Outside my own mother's
roof, I do not know of any other roof I would want to spend time under than that of my hon. friend.

The minister would be safe
there.

Earlier in the week a press
dispatch indicated that there was some thought of using the Pacific Coast Militia Rangers for civil defence duties. I do not know whether the Minister of National Health and Welfare would know anything about that or whether it comes entirely under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Defence. But this dispatch stated that there would be a reorganization of that group which contained about 16,000 men during the last war, and also that they would be doing civil defence work. Can either of the ministers tell me whether or not that dispatch is correct, and just what plans have been made; also whether any steps have been taken to reconstitute the civilian observer corps?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Perhaps that is a question which should be addressed to the Minister of National Defence. Would the hon. member mind waiting until we have completed the civil defence discussion? While it has a civil defence aspect, it really goes much beyond that. Perhaps he would care to wait and deal with it later, so that we could deal with the civil defence matter first.
The dispatch says that the duties they are to undertake are civil defence duties. Presumably, therefore, they would come under the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
As I said, they have a civil defence aspect. But undoubtedly, as I said this afternoon, there is the other aspect. For instance, we have made arrangements to


use the detection service of the Ontario department of forestry. They have a vast army-perhaps I should not say it is a vast army-but very efficient operation groups of forest fire observers, as the leader of the opposition knows much better than I do, one that serves in outlying posts and in all forest areas. We will be using them. But I thought that my hon. friend was taking the matter from another angle; and I thought from that other angle, in so far as it applied to the Department of National Defence, he might care to wait until we dealt with the purely national defence items.
If this group are to be used, there would have to be a reorganization. It is not like using a body that is already functioning.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am aware of that.
Can the Minister of National Defence say whether they are taking steps to reorganize them, or under which department would that reorganization come?

The Pacific Coast Rangers which did an extremely useful job during the war were reorganized in 1947 as the Canadian Rangers. Now they have companies operating from end to end of Canada. Their role is primarily to supplement that of the active and1 reserve forces of Canada, but they have civil defence roles as well. So far, there are twenty-one companies organized and they form a component of the Canadian army reserve. They are being organized just as rapidly as we can organize them in every part where there is no ordinary reserve army unit. Their jobs are to provide guides to organized troops within their own area; coast watching; assistance to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and provincial police in the discovery, reporting and apprehension of enemy agents or saboteurs; the reporting of other suspicious activities; immediate local defence against sabotage by small enemy detachments or saboteurs and to assist and augment civilian protective arrangements against saboteurs, within the area in which the organization is authorized to operate; reporting, locating and rescue work, including first aid treatment in connection with aircraft in distress.
These Canadian Rangers are organized on much the same basis as the Pacific Coast Rangers. I remember that I took part at the inauguration of this plan in 1947. General Worthington, who is the co-ordinator of civil defence, is the honorary colonel commandant of the corps of Canadian Rangers, and that organization is proceeding.
I am glad to hear that. They certainly did splendid work during the last war. Apparently they come under the Department of National Defence. How many have been enlisted?

The present establishment is set at 5,000. I have not that information as to the exact number enlisted. As I say, they are organized in twenty-one companies; and from a map I have seen in the northwestern command, they cover fairly well the whole area of the Northwest Territories, the Arctic, the coast of British Columbia, and are now extending over the Hudson bay area and the north Atlantic coast.
What about the Canadian air observer corps? Is that a separate corps?

It is under organization now under the Royal Canadian Air Force. There is not anything yet in addition to the organization plan. I do not want to minimize it because we want to get everyone in it that we can; but, on the other hand, its utility with regard to aircraft that may be flying at 20,000 feet or more is limited. Nevertheless, its utility in connection with landings is very important.

I am sure the minister will pardon me, but I think he made a slip of the tongue when he said that these Canadian Rangers were being organized in every part of Canada. Surely they are being organized only in those northern areas where there are no militia units.
That is right.
The minister's first statement was "in every part of Canada", which would give the impression that they were being organized in the settled parts of Canada.
The hon. member is quite right. I think the record will indicate that I said it was being organized where there are no organized reserve army units. The hon. member is quite right.

Mr. Chairman, I was not particularly happy with the answer the minister gave me this afternoon to my question on civil defence in Newfoundland, and I should like to refer to it again if he would not mind. From what I could gather, either the information was such that the pipe line between himself and the civil defence authorities has a poor coupling or else the pressure is such that the information does not get through to him. It certainly does not get past him because it is not made public to the province. As I believe the minister knows, the situation is this. Some time in the early part of the 80709-219
Supply-National Defence year, an extremely public-spirited gentleman was appointed director of civil defence. He is fully aware of that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Curtis, was it not?

No; Mr. F. M. O'Leary. He came to Ottawa and attended meetings up here. Following that, he went home and shortly afterwards resigned. In his explanation he said that apparently the authorities at home were not taking the matter of civil defence seriously and were not prepared to co-operate with him. Since that time, as far as the public is concerned, nothing has happened. Today the minister said that under Mr. Curtis, the attorney general, there is a committee of five working. They may be working, but so far as the public or the province is concerned no plans have been outlined and nothing has been done. I should like the minister to tell me if he knows something that we have not been able to find out yet.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I cannot add anything to what I said this afternoon. The civil defence minister, Hon. L. R. Curtis, I am sure is a gentleman of great perspicacity and one who is greatly concerned about this matter, as I am sure my hon. friend is. I have no doubt but that he will pursue this with the same diligence with which it is being pursued in all provinces.
He must be hiding his light under a bushel.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Ministers sometimes do that.

I think this debate which has now lasted for several hours has brought home to the committee the seriousness with which hon. members on all sides view this very important subject of civil defence. The minister himself stressed its importance. He has emphasized various aspects, including the need for co-operation at the various levels of government in the plans that are now beginning to be worked out; the need for the support of everyone throughout the land in order to make these plans effective, and so on. The minister has pointed out that it is not the amount of money allocated to this branch of defence that is the prime factor; yet as he went on he discussed the need of equipment, the need to develop communications services, and the need for greater personnel. So I think it will be obvious to everyone that before this plan can go into effect much larger sums of money will be required in order to make it really effective. I think we can assure the minister from this side of the house that we realize the importance of this work, and that if cooperation is required it will be forthcoming to the fullest possible extent.

Supply-National Defence

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Thank you.

We shall do everything we can. I come back for a moment to a point I made earlier and upon which the minister touched. It is contained in this excellent pamphlet the minister has issued, in which it says that the effectiveness of the civil defence system will depend in the first instance upon an adequate warning system. We realize that. The minister has told us how in the course of the last twenty-four hours steps have been taken to obtain the co-operation of the communications companies of this country. Obviously they are working toward these ends. Perhaps the minister should not be as emphatic as he was last night in pointing out what he thought were certain inaccuracies in what I had said, particularly when I mentioned that an adequate warning system did not exist at the moment.
I have just one other comment to make. In this pamphlet considerable stress is laid upon providing shock-resisting features, fire prevention requirements, basements suitable for shelters and so on in any construction work being carried out. We know a great deal of construction is being carried on by the dominion government, some of it by the Department of National Defence. That department is erecting married quarters and barracks for single men in strategic centres which might be considered likely targets by the enemy. I hope these suggestions in regard to providing basements which can be converted into shelters will be noted by the Minister of National Defence, and that where these barracks blocks are being constructed consideration will be given to these matters. That has not been the case in the past; there are no basement shelters now. As construction goes on I hope those things will be provided. As I said before, I think we have underlined the importance of civil defence, and I do not intend to pursue the subject further.

One question was brought to my mind by the remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo. In outlining these specific expenditures for civil defence the minister mentioned the sum of $350,000 for the acquisition and construction of buildings and works including the acquisition of land. Is that intended for administration buildings, or is it to make a start on some type of shelter, or is it for experimentation in regard to shelters, or what is it for?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
That was intended for a
structure to house the technical training school now in operation at Connaught Ranges. While I am on my feet I might give the hon. member some information I could not give a

short time ago. The $20,000 for communications equipment will be used largely for a certain type of walkie-talkie set that has been found useful in this work. I only want to say to the hon. member for Nanaimo that in the spirit of understanding he has shown I thank him for his offer of co-operation which in any event, apart from his declaration, I was sure would be forthcoming.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreed that the debate on civil defence is now concluded?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the sub-item carry?
Sub-item agreed to.
Professional and special services, $200,000.
Could we have an explanation of this?

I observe that the same amount is allocated to this sub-item this year as last year. Would the minister give us a breakdown of the purposes for which this money is spent and the persons by whom it is received?

This has to do with inspection service. It provides for inspection by commercial firms, to which I referred last night; the U.S. navy, the U.K. government and Canadian Arsenals Limited; also for payment to the Canadian Commercial Corporation on a pro rata basis for the Canadian corps of commissionaires required for security purposes at No. 2 building, Ottawa. The details are armaments branch, guns and carriages, motor transport, ammunition, $75,000; technical services branches, chemicals, $10,000; ships branch, material, $92,000; clothing stores branch, textiles and barracks stores, $22,400; Canadian corps of commissionaires, to which I have already referred, $600. The figure is the same as for last year, and is all related to professional services in relation to inspection.
I understand these are commercial firms which are employed in addition to the inspectors paid under the preceding item about which we had a good deal of discussion?
That is right, except that we also pay the U.S. navy, the U.K. government and Canadian Arsenals Limited as well as the corps of commissionaires that small amount of $600.
Would the minister tell the committee what kind of service the Canadian Commercial Corporation renders this department for which it has to pay under the administration item?
We share a building with C.C.C. and pay half the cost of guarding the building by the corps of commissionaires.

Well, I may have misunderstood the minister. I understood he said the department pays $600 to the corps of commissionaires. That was one item. Then, there were three large items on which I thought he said that either the $92,000 or the $22,400 went to the Canadian Commercial Corporation.

No, I am sorry. The only
payment under this is to the Canadian corps of commissionaires $600 for half the cost of guarding the building which we share with the Canadian Commercial Corporation.
I am sorry that I did not keep up with the minister. Will the minister tell me again what the $22,400 item is?

Clothing and stores branch,
textiles and bag stores, $22,400. It is paid to outside inspectors to inspect these items.
That is, the Canadian Commercial Corporation were making sure for the department that the clothing ordered is up to standard?
That is right.
Are there any oculists employed or paid under this item?

No; the only oculists that
we have would be under the payments for the navy, army and air force, votes for medical services.

I have a matter I want to
discuss under this item, sir. I do not know of any other way in which I can do so except under this particular item. To me, it is an important matter. At'the annual meeting of the Canadian Tuberculosis Association held in Toronto between May 7 and 11, there was a very interesting discussion concerning the use of BCG and the tuberculin testing of recruits for the services. Arising out of that discussion, which I may say was participated in by doctors from all across the country, a resolution was passed. Really, it was the adoption of the resolution of the management committee, which had been passed and sent to the Minister of National Defence in September of last year. I should like to have this resolution inscribed, Mr. Chairman, so that you can follow the matter. The resolution reads as follows:
Whereas the tuberculosis control program throughout Canada has led to a marked Increase in the numbers of negative reactors and whereas it is acknowledged that through contact with infectious tuberculosis the chances of negative tuberculin reactors developing tuberculosis is materially greater than otherwise; and whereas a negative X-ray plate can provide no Indication of the tuberculin status of the individual, therefore, the Canadian Tuberculosis
80709-219J
Supply-National Defence
Association recommends that the tuberculin status be determined by the use of the tuberculin test at the time of enlistment examination, and if possible, extended to all service personnel at present enlisted. In further support of this resolution, consideration is given to the increased risk of tuberculosis infection in countries other than Canada and the United States, and the consequent influence on pensionable cases resulting from such circumstance.
The association regrets that the Department of National Defence has not seen fit, up to the present, to adopt this procedure. The C.T.A. urges that prompt action be taken in this matter, considering the present world situation.
The Canadian Tuberculosis Association also endorsed a further resolution of the management committee dated September 25, 1950, which reads as follows:
That, whereas the number of negative tuberculin reactors in the recruiting ages is rapidly increasing, and whereas this situation means an increased susceptibility to tuberculosis, and whereas such people if sent in the course of duty to countries where infectious tuberculosis is much more prevalent than at home, and whereas BCG vaccination of negative tuberculin does provide an appreciable degree of protection against the development of tuberculosis, therefore the Canadian Tuberculosis Association recommends that negative tuberculin reactors be vaccinated with BCG vaccine to reduce the hazard of tuberculosis as experienced in the course of duty.
Now, Mr. Chairman., both of those resolutions were adopted by the management committee of the Canadian Tuberculosis Association on September 25, 1950. They were both communicated to the Minister of National Defence at that time; and, as I understand, the reasons were given for those resolutions being passed. The minister was urged to follow the course suggested by the resolutions. Up to the present at least no action has been taken in the matter. I understand, though I do not know of my own knowledge, that the medical men of the services are in full accord with this program. Certainly, all the doctors that were present at that annual meeting, as I say, doctors from all across the dominion, thoroughly approved of it. The suggestion is that sending recruits, say to Korea, without proper testing is sending them into very great danger indeed of contracting tuberculosis if they have not been inoculated with BCG.
I am told that the cost is very, very little indeed. The cost of testing, and the cost of inoculating with BCG would be less than ten cents per recruit. The time required is, I believe, not more than forty-eight hours. I understand that negative reactors to the tuberculin tests, when they have received an inoculation from BCG, have more or less about 90 per cent protecr tion against contracting tuberculosis. Now, Mr. Chairman, when we take into account, not only the humanitarian principle involved but the possibility of boys and young men
3434	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence being inducted into the forces without proper protection against this germ, that of itself is a very strong appeal indeed. Then, when we look at the financial part of it, and when we look at the huge amount that must be paid out for pensions for those who have contracted tuberculosis while in the armed services, the cost of sanatorium treatment for them, then indeed it becomes a very serious problem. I understand that in the last war when the men from provinces which have a very low incidence of tuberculosis, such as Saskatchewan, were exposed to tuberculosis in the course of their duties, they picked it up much quicker than those from provinces which had a higher incidence of the disease.
For that reason, Mr. Chairman, it strikes me as being of the utmost importance that these recommendations of the Canadian Tuberculosis Association should be adopted. I see no reason at all, no excuse on the ground of delay, in getting the men into the forces or on the ground of the costs. In fact, I cannot see any grounds at all for not following that course. I am told that the minister's idea is that this should be a more or less voluntary decision on the part of a recruit, whether or not he will submit to it. Many hon. members are fully aware of what the ordinary recruit would do if such a proposition were put to him. I suggest quite definitely to the minister that this program should be adopted, and there should not be any question of its being voluntary. It should be a compulsory inoculation at the time the recruit is inducted. I should like to hear a comment from the minister.

I can appreciate the representations put forward by the hon. member for St. John's East. I think it was in 1944 or 1945, when I had the honour of being Minister of National Health and Welfare, that we introduced the BCG through Dr. Frappier, particularly in connection with the prevention or arrest of tuberculosis among Indians. The area in which the tests were first conducted by us on a large scale in Canada was in Qu'Appelle in the province of Saskatchewan. That was in 1945, I think. Then I also became familiar with this in Paris in 1946, at the Pasteur institute and in other places had representations made to me about it. Canada has made good progress in this direction.
In the province of Quebec, my own province, this testing or inoculation is carried out particularly with young infants, and it seems to have been very successful.
With regard to personnel in the armed forces, we have X-rays and very careful


medical examinations. The incidence of tuberculosis among members of the armed forces is small. There are some risks and uncertainties involved, but we are in close consultation with the Canadian Tuberculosis Association, the Department of National Health and Welfare, particularly, and the great expert of Canada, Dr. Wherrett. We shall be very glad to take into consideration the representations of my hon. friend.

As I recall, the minister said that in connection with the vote of $200,000 the amount of $75,000 was for inspection in the manufacture of guns, commercial inspection. It is quite a large item. I did not keep up with the minister in my notes but, as I recall, it was for that purpose. Can the minister give us the relationship between what is paid for this type of inspection of armament production and the quite large number of inspectors within the department, of whom we just heard 727 are paid under the vote that we have just passed? If we are paying these people-and I think it is quite important that we should have at any rate inspection of production of our armaments-why then, if we have these presumably well qualified people who are in the various plants producing for us, should we in addition have to pay for professional and special services? Why should we have to pay other people to do the same work?

I think the answer to the
hon. member is that this payment, which is relatively small, in view of the amount spent in inspection, and also the amount spent for equipment, is due to two causes. Either we have peak loads where we have a shipment of arms to another country on a special order, or else we are producing arms on the orders of another country such as the United States or the United Kingdom and we pay their inspector to inspect for us as well as for themselves; and of course we either give the goods away or else collect the amount in the total payment we receive.

Do I understand that this
would be in the nature of a contingency as though perhaps the 727 people who it is anticipated will be paid during the coming year out of the vote we have just passed may not be enough to do the various jobs that we may be called upon to do, or it may be necessary to employ outside people? Is that the nature of this particular portion of this $200,000? Is it in the nature of a contingency fund?

Part of this amount would
be paid for the inspection by the United States individual inspectors of equipment that we buy in the United States, which is

delivered to us. The other element is payment to Canadian inspecting Arms to take care of peak loads and is contingent, based on our experience during the past year.

If it is a contingent item to
an extent, at any rate, what was the expenditure last year?-because I observe that the estimates for the two years are the same.

We have the expenditures
estimated for the year 1950-51-the books are not closed yet-in primaries, but we have not got that broken down because the bills have not all been added up. I can get that for the hon. member.

Will the minister say a word
or two in enlargement of the general situation that there are peak loads where I understand it is necessary to employ outside personnel? Is it considered that it is not efficient or possible to anticipate just how many inspectional personnel you need in the department, permanent staff, to be paid out of the item "civil salaries and wages"? Would it be considered less efficient to employ enough persons to provide for this contingency, and estimate accordingly in the first sub-item, rather than providing this fairly large sum of $200,000 for unforeseen contingencies? If we are to have this contingency, to what extent are we unable to anticipate it?

We have a good deal of difficulty in anticipating them, because this year we will be spending several hundred million dollars on equipment; and how much we get from the manufacturers at any time depends on some events outside our own control.
Now, if we maintain an inspection staff sufficient to deal with the peak, then it will be uneconomical because they will be unemployed at certain times. Also, we cannot anticipate when the peaks will occur, because they may depend on the flow of United States components in Canadian equipment. Therefore, in some instances it is more economical to employ outside inspectors to supplement our own inside inspectors rather than to keep a large staff going and not have them fully employed the year round.

I think that is a reasonable
explanation. Would the minister then be able to tell me where he would turn for this type of inspection services? Can he give us, for instance, the names of some of the firms he employed? Can he give us the names of those he employed to inspect delivery of guns? May I put a concrete question? Surely the minister would not employ the inspector from the firm which is making the
Supply-National Defence guns? Where does he find these people? How is he able to pick them out so as to employ them and to turn them on to somebody else's produce?

There are a considerable number of firms with professional standing who do this kind of work. I could not, quite frankly, give the hon. member details as to our employment of any of these firms in the year ahead. But there are such firms as Warnock, in the field of mechanical engineering, and Rankin; and J. T. Donald and Company in the field of chemicals.
And for clothing?
I do not think we would use one for clothing. We have our own inspectors for clothing.
I thought the minister told us that one of the components of the $200,000 was for the inspection of clothing.

I gave the figure of $22,400 for clothing and stores branch, technical and barracks stores. I would be surprised to hear that our inspectors do not inspect all the clothing. It may be possible that we might employ an outside firm to help us over a peak load. We have had several peak loads. However, I will look into that.
Sub-item agreed to.
Defence services-
Travelling and removal expenses, $379,000.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks. I am going to ask the minister whether this item provides far officers to take ladies to cocktail parties when off duty. Before he answers I wish to bring to his attention certain facts. The hon. member for Fraser Valley in the public accounts committee, as well as some other hon. members, directed the attention of the committee to the fact that army cars were being used improperly, at times, and brought certain incidents to the attention of the deputy minister, who was a witness at the time.
The deputy minister replied that a series of checks was made, on occasions, or generally, and that the system was, that if a private soldier who was driving a general who used an army vehicle improperly cares to report that general, he may do so. Well, I can see a private reporting a general! That would be the end of the private.
I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the Vancouver Sun of May 19, which contains a whole page which apparently is intended as a build-up for the army's gala ball. The heading is, "Army Polishes up for Gala Ball". It shows a type of advertising

Supply-National Defence and pictures that would make Cromwell turn over in his grave. We see in the top picture a luscious beauty in evening dress reclining, somewhat after the fashion of Cleopatra. She is reclining in a most languid manner while being shown, the operation of a machine gun. I cannot believe that that would add much to the Canadian recruiting drive.
Oh, I think so.

One would think we were trying to defend a Hail-Hail-The-Gang's-All-Here sort of civilization. I wish to bring to the attention of the minister particularly another picture about six inches by eight inches in size. This is the picture of a jeep in which there are two officers andi two attractive looking women. Under the picture it says:
The army has never been the same since the first jeep was built. The busy little vehicle plays a dozen important roles in its military career, but here's a brand new one. This gay foursome has commandeered one for party transportation as they attend a pre-military ball affair.
I made inquiries as to what the "premilitary ball affair" was, and I am informed it was a pre-military ball cocktail party.
What is that?
A cocktail party prior to a military ball.
Oh.

But my point is this, that we see in this picture an army vehicle paid for out of public money, and operated with gasoline paid for at public expense, which would possibly be meeting workers coming out of plants, workers with lunch buckets in their hands. Does that build up morale- when they are being asked to pay 20 per cent surtax only to have officers and their wives or friends ride around in government jeeps and government property, as the picture indicates? And it is not only this picture, but if hon. members would look at the Vancouver Province of May 19, the same date, they would see another picture of a jeep showing two army officers and two other ladies being invited in to have a ride. Apparently in that case however the ladies thought it would be rough riding, and they did not go.
This indicates however that these army vehicles are being used for other than army purposes in off-duty periods. There is much more of that going on in. this country than, I am sure, the minister realizes. What would be the attitude of a working woman walking down the street and seeing these people, who live at a very high standard compared with
[Mr. Herridge.}

that of the average worker-people dressed in furs and frills riding down the street in an army jeep at public expense?
Then, in addition to that, a gentleman came to me out of the gallery of this chamber this afternoon and told me he was from Montreal. He said, "I have been interested in this discussion"-and he was referring to questions asked by hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party, sitting to my right. He said to me, "My near neighbour is a provost marshal in Montreal, and you can tell the minister for me that that gentleman, regardless of what the deputy minister says, has his children driven to a private school every morning in an army car, by an army chauffeur, and brought home every night in that army car by the army chauffeur, and taken on week-end trips at the country's expense."
I would like the minister to explain why these vehicles are used on those occasions, and if that is permitted under army regulations, and under his administration.

I think I know what the hon. member is referring to. I saw that in the paper, but I do not think he is making it clear. Was that not when -the new brigadier was taking over command in British Columbia at Vancouver?
No, this was for the pregala ball party.

If the hon. member would look at it he would see that the ladies are in evening dress, and that the jeep was just photographed for the purposes of the newspaper. It is only a little bit of advertising of the officers ball on that occasion, and I suggest the hon. member should not have brought it up in the way that he has, or should not have made the suggestion that it is being driven around Vancouver for that purpose.
The newspaper says so.
I know it says so-but you know what newspapers are.
It is in the Vancouver Sun.

I am obliged to the hon. member for Kootenay West who has brought this matter to my attention. First, with regard to the officer in the provost corps at Montreal, if what the hon. member says is so, then I must say it is strictly against regulations and will be dealt with accordingly. I shall look into it.
Thank you.

Then, with regard to the occasion to which he has referred1, and to

this picture of officers, and others, attending an army ball-well, I do not know; I am not terribly familiar with those things.
Oh, oh.

But I should think that anyone who was would recognize at once that these pictures were taken with some view to having them appear in a social column or some other column of a newspaper for publicity purposes.
I am not too sure they are bad publicity; that is a question of opinion. Perhaps I might think they are bad or good publicity while others might not. I saw this, and looked into it, and I am assured, with regard to this picture of the two officers and their wives in the jeep, that the picture was taken in the armoury at the request of the photographer of the Vancouver Sun and that, for the purpose, the jeep was backed up against the wall of the armoury, and not one ounce of gasoline was used.

I have been totalling up the
travelling and removal expenses and freight, express and cartage for the army, navy and air force and I find it comes to about $32 million. How does the department divide this business between the two main railroads?

I could look up the traffic
for 1950-51, but as I remember it is almost 50-50. Where one railroad provides a better service, we use that railroad. Where there are alternative services available an attempt at equalization is made. As I remember, and I do not necessarily indicate the exact figures, it was about $1,500,000 for one and $1,400,000 for the other.
Sub-item agreed to.
Telephones, telegrams and other communication services, $26,500.

I understand that the army
has a special telephone service of its own, and under army a large sum of money is provided for that purpose, well over $1 million. Under headquarters we have this item of $26,500 which apparently is paid for services other than those provided by the army. Is that paid to civilian companies? Does the army service the administration branch of the department?

This amount of $26,500 is
paid to outside telephone and telegraph agencies. The total cost of the tri-service communications system is far greater than that. I would say that 95 per cent of all communications by telegraph or radioteletype between the three services are carried across Canada by tri-service communications set-up.
This service went into effect at the beginning of last year. The navy, army and air
Supply-National Defence force cover all the main centres of Canada on a 24 hour basis. There is no duplication. The navy operates the terminals at Esquimau and Halifax, the army operate in Montreal, the air force in Winnipeg and so on. The service duplicates to a considerable degree the existing commercial services across Canada. There are between 1,500 and 2,000 personnel involved. In addition to carrying almost all the traffic for the armed forces a good deal of traffic is carried for other government departments. As indicated before, during emergencies this service is used to carry commercial traffic as well.
The service is almost fully occupied today and is capable of carrying a heavier load in the event of war. We consider it essential to maintain it in peacetime and keep it built up so it wiU be available in the event of war.
It has the most modern equipment. There is some radioteletype and some line-teletype, and the whole system is connected with similar systems in the United States, Great Britain, Australia and throughout the world. It carries all ordinary traffic that can be sent by wire.
In addition to the operations of the magnitude I have indicated it is necessary for many telephone calls to be sent out, and this vote of $26,500 is necessary. For instance, there may be a conference of senior officers or a collecting of last-minute recruiting returns. Telephone calls may even be necessary in order to answer parliamentary inquiries. There is an increase of only $1,700 over last year.

This is most interesting
because I believe this is the first official announcement, certainly the first in parliament, of the establishment of this triservice communications system. Has it been used in time of national emergency, such as the emergency which caused the special session of parliament last year?

I am not so sure that it was used in connection with the emergency that necessitated the special session, but it was used in a major way in connection with the Fraser valley floods. The ordinary commercial communications broke down and the services took over and carried all communications into the Fraser valley and also into Vancouver to a considerable degree as well as to many other areas. 1 remember authorizing the dispatch of 23 operators by air from Montreal in order to help to carry the load. For several days most personal and commercial traffic was carried by this service.
The same thing occurred during the Winnipeg flood, but to a minor degree. During a snowslide in British Columbia the same thing occurred. I remember visiting one of
3438	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence these stations in Winnipeg and I was told that it had carried commercial traffic, including 20,000 words for the Canadian Press, during the previous 24 hours. There was a breakdown in the maritime services and our service carried everything for 24 hours for both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National telegraph systems. It has been of great value in meeting civilian emergencies.
It meets all service needs. We carry thousands of messages each month for other government departments. All communications with the Northwest Territories and the Arctic are carried by this service.

When the service is used by other government departments do they pay for that? Would the Canadian Press pay for what service they obtained, and would the Canadian Pacific pay for what messages of theirs were carried?
Other government departments do not pay, but commercial users would unless the message was carried on compassionate grounds.

I appreciate fully the value of this tri-service system in the event of war or national emergency and I realize the importance of having it maintained with trained personnel, but I wonder if the minister can give any indication as to how the cost of maintaining such a service would compare with the cost of using similar civilian transcontinental services?

I am afraid I would not be able to obtain an equivalent figure for the civilian services. But it is not competitive in a real sense because we engage in training personnel, operating in isolated centres, operating non-commercial routes. I am afraid, therefore, that I could hot give any comparison. It has just been suggested to me that the cost would be higher because of security requirements. Over this system we can carry all kinds of security restricted messages which could not be carried over commercial systems but which require processing through the ordinary ciphering and deciphering equipment and so on.
Is there any duplication at all in connection with the government telephone services which are also provided in remote parts of this country under the Department of Transport?

Following the inquiry that was made, I think in the public accounts committee, we have looked into the matter and we can find no duplication at all.
Sub-item agreed to.
Printing of departmental reports and other publications, $122,500.

I notice that this particular item is a little bit more than twice what it was last year. I was wondering if the minister could tell us what the reason for this increase is and what publications and departmental reports this item covers other than this report of the Department of National Defence which we all received. I ask that question particularly because I notice that the same item appears in the navy, the army and the air force, and quite large sums are involved in each of those branches. I was wondering exactly what was covered by this particular item so far as headquarters is concerned, the administrative department.

In answer to the hon. member, I can say that almost all the increase is accounted for by the fact that this year we are providing quite a considerable item for civil defence in the estimates of this department. The amount provided for 1950-51 was $60,000. The amount now asked for is $122,500. The increase is $62,500. Of the increase, $51,500 is applicable to civil defence, so that only $11,000 is applicable to the Department of National Defence, and that is owing to the increase in activities and the expansion of the size of the department.

What other publications are put out, so far as headquarters are concerned, besides this report on national defence? This year the only other thing I have seen is "Canada's Defence Program" which is practically a reprint of the minister's speech on February 5 in this house, with a little addition to it. What other publications are put out besidesi those two?

In the department we issue a good many appeals for support; that is, requests for support for the work of the armed forces. For instance, there was a letter I recently addressed to over 3,500 or more employers asking them to support the work of the armed forces of Canada. I believe that comes out of this item. During the year there are a good many similar letters or appeals that require to be issued in that way. There are no other major items. This is made up of a multitude of small items.

As the hon. member for Calgary East has pointed out, this same item is duplicated in other parts of the departmental estimates. To be specific, it is duplicated seven times, and the total of those other seven items is in the neighbourhood of $2 million. That makes me wonder whether this could not be done in another way. For instance, at page 270 the navy has an item of $344,000; the army has an item of $495,000; and air has an item of $1,049,000; under

aerial photographic survey there is an item of $1,650; and under defence research and development there is an item of $100,550, to name some of the larger ones.
I should like to ask whether any of these sums and any of the sum before us of $122,500 is in connection with the recruiting program. Whether it is or whether it is not, I should like to know why all the various departmental reports-because the wording of the item is "printing of departmental reports and other publications"-are not centralized under the departmental administration. It occurs to me, at first sight at any rate, that for the army to have a separate publications branch and for the navy, the air force, defence research and development, and aerial photographic survey each to have a separate one, is something that indicates a little bit of inefficiency. It appears to me that if each of these was to be centralized, a more efficient, a more closely interrelated, and probably a less expensive job could be done. I come back to the point that these other seven items in the department total $2 million.

I can understand the hon. member's difficulty. But the printing is not done by the navy, the army and the air force. All printing contracts are placed by the service concerned, through the deputy minister's office, with the king's printer or under his authority with some outside printer. There is no competition and no inefficiency of administration. The printing of course amounts to a large sum, as the hon. member knows, having been an officer himself.
Does it include all departments?

It includes a lot of work instruction books, drill books, pamphlets, training manuals and the like. Each service is responsible for the production of the material for those, but the order for their printing is placed, through the deputy minister, with the king's printer or, through him, with an outside printer. That is subject to few exceptions, in respect of which we do some printing within the department itself, largely relating to security material. When you consider that this relates to the three services, and the defence research board, which has a good deal of printing of restricted material to do, you can understand why it appears under seven headings.

I understand the minister to say that the only control or co-ordination is through the deputy minister. These various branches or services put their requirements up and they go through the deputy minister
Supply-National Defence who, I presume, must approve them. I am just wondering whether it would not be better to have a central office. Since you have an item under departmental administration, I am wondering whether it would not be better to have that office, as it were, coordinating all the printing requirements. Does it include, for instance, such things as 'the part II orders of the various services?

No; part II orders are
mimeographed. Naval service orders, army orders and air force orders are printed through the king's printer but all the subordinate orders are done in mimeographed form.
But these various items would cover the cost of that, would they not?
Yes.
The words "other publications" are quite wide. Does this include anything in connection with recruiting?

I take it my hon. friend is
now referring to item 9 in the summary of standard objects. That does not include recruiting, which is the next item, No. 10, which deals with films, displays, broadcasting, advertising, and so on.

I do not want to anticipate
that item, but there is no item 10 under departmental administration.
That is right.

I do not want to anticipate
another branch or item that will come later, but I do suggest that national defence headquarters should control the recruiting program and its set-up, whereas we find it broken down under army, navy and air force. How does that work?

We are anticipating, but I
am very glad to do it. To deal with recruiting for the three services we have set up under the direction of the personnel members committee an interservice recruiting committee. As hon. members may recall, the personnel members committee consists of the heads of personnel of the three services. In the case of the navy it is the chief naval personnel, the CNP as he is called. In the case of the army it is the adjutant general, and in the case of the air force the air *member for personnel. This committee deals with all personnel matters affecting the three services, including recruiting. Subordinate to them is the joint service recruiting committee and the joint service advertising committee consisting of officers appointed to represent the navy, army and air members of PMC. They make recommendations to PMC in regard to recruiting

Supply-National Defence matters. We have at least two general sessions a year, which I usually attend as do the members of the PMC, the joint services recruiting committee and the advertising agencies concerned. We draw up programs for recruiting advertising. Those programs are modified and changed from week to week and month to month, because this is a very sensitive operation; but there is complete tri-service co-operation.
Once the recruiting plan has been agreed to as between the three services and approved by myself, we work it out in financial terms. There is a financial adjustment, which is almost always downward, and the actual procedure of accounting is handled through the deputy minister. So there is complete unified control of the whole operation from start to finish.

I will not pursue that at the moment beyond saying it seems a little odd that the expense should be allotted to the services, which must be rather arbitrary, instead of the over-all recruiting program being accounted for under departmental administration. However, that detail can be discussed later.
I should like to follow up the same point, if I may, in connection with item No. 9 in the general summary of standard objects, which is the printing of departmental reports and other publications. How do you decide which service will have so much money to spend; or why is it not simply decided that so much money will be allowed for the printing of departmental reports and publications and put that money under departmental administration. From there on you could control the expenditure by each branch of the service so the total amount would not be overspent.

We are dealing only with
administration at present, and as the hon. member can see the increase is very small.

Of that $51,500 is applicable to civil defence, which we did not have at all in the previous year. To answer the other question as to the build-up of budgets, of course we get into a pretty big field there. Each service builds up the budget for that service. It plans its work for the year ahead, in fact for three years ahead. It discusses those plans with the other services in the chiefs of staff committee and at other levels. The deputy minister or his representative sits in at all those discussions, and common factors for the build-up of all the budget elements are agreed to so that it is worked out that a man in the army will cost as much as a man in the air force doing the same

job, and so on. All those things are pretty well worked out now, and we have very good methods of computing costs.
With regard to manpower, they relate this to the expected build-up through the year month by month, and increase or decrease the grants for pay and allowances accordingly. The same thing is done with regard to food, and so on, averaged out for the year. Then they look ahead and see what construction is needed, and this is considered so as not to be out of line with the other services. Equipment is the biggest and most difficult element. We have endless sessions from about August to November within the department working on our own estimates as between the three service heads and the deputy minister, and finally with myself, but always in consultation with representatives of the treasury. Ultimately we bring forward to the cabinet defence committee a plan for the next year, and that is discussed at a good many meetings. They settle on a plan; then we go back and cost that plan, and having costed it put it forward to the defence committee again, and bring it on to the cabinet. Then it enters into the estimates.
That is the process followed in every country, as far as I know. It is very convenient to have it done under the heads of the navy, army and air force, each keeping their own figures, making their own estimates and looking after their own appropriations; and that is all done subject to tri-service co-operation and- departmental control through the deputy minister. I know of no other country where it is so unified as in our case, where we have a single vote, a single deputy minister, a single minister and a single department.

The only other question I
think I will ask on this has to do with a comparison between the vote this year and last year. This shows here that the vote for 1950-51 was $60,000, but when I look at the estimates for last year under departmental administration, the only place where I can find figures for the corresponding item is under the sundries item, where it states that sundries including printing and stationery, et cetera, amounted to $186,637. Is that $60,000 the amount which was extracted from the $186,000 which was for printing?
Yes, that is right.
Is that an estimate or an actual expenditure?
It is an estimate.
Have you got the figure for the expenditure as yet?
Not yet.

Mr. Chairman, in connection with this $122,000, $51,500 is for civil defence or something along that line, which leaves $71,000. So far as I can make out that $71,000 was the expenditure for printing this report of the Department of National Defence, the odd white paper such as this one which was issued a short time ago, and the printing of a few thousand form letters which the minister sends out from time to time. It seems to me that is a great deal of money for these printing activities. Can the minister tell us what the actual cost of printing this report of the Department of National Defence was?

That is done by the king's printer, and it would not cost very much. But the inspection services, for example, which have to provide technical specifications with regard to a great number of items would be provided for out of this item.

This is for the printing of reports and other publications. From everything the minister said before, I have certainly understood it was to cover the cost of printing this report, these white papers and some form letters that he sends out from time to time. Surely, this does not cover inspection services of any sort.

This is the ninth of the headings laid down by the -treasury board for the uniform presentation of estimates to parliament. This is the first year this has been done, and we have conformed to the system laid down. This is item 9, and we have put under it items that the treasury told us should be put under that item.
What are they, then, besides the actual printing of these reports?

That is the printing for the department, not paid for by the navy, army or air force; the report, the circular letters; printing by the inspection services, and by the director of public relations for the department.
Any speeches?
None at all.

Mr. Chairman, I am still rather in the dark as to what these other items of printing are in addition to the reports and letters the minister has mentioned, as well as the odd white paper. What
Supply-National Defence printing would be put out, so far as the administration branch is concerned, by those people he has mentioned?
I shall be glad to get that information for you.

Office stationery, supplies and equipment, $111,000.
Mr. Chairman, in connection with films, displays, advertising and other informational publicity-
No, it is office stationery.
I am talking about the films, displays and advertising-
On what page is that?
I am on page 271.

We are on page 269.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on
Monday we shall revert to legislation and take up Bill No. 198, an act to amend the Customs Act. It is in committee, and we have completed about half of it. Then, we shall take up Bill No. 293, an act respecting units of length and mass; then Bill No. 191, an act to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act; Bill No. 192, an act to amend the Petition of Right Act; Bill No. 338, an act to amend the Quebec Savings Banks Act; the resolution in the name of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) to amend the Veterans Insurance Act; the bill respecting the Canada post office. If we were fortunate enough to be able to complete that business, I would move to go into supply and call three departments.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
